articles.body:
Ministro Kassio Nunes Marques — Foto: Luiz Roberto/TSE

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), Nunes Marques, decidiu nesta quarta-feira (25) criar um grupo de trabalho para mapear as principais dificuldades e elaborar uma proposta com medidas de prevenção para garantir o enfrentamento do crime organizado nas eleições.

🔎 O avanço das facções e de milícias no processo eleitoral é apontado como uma das principais preocupações da Justiça Eleitoral. O TSE tem impedido desde as eleições de 2024 que pessoas ligadas a facções criminosas participem das eleições sob argumento de que a Constituição Federal proíbe o uso de organizações paramilitares por partidos políticos.

Na disputa deste ano, o Ministério Público Eleitoral (MPE) questionou 42 candidaturas em 10 estados por ligação de políticos com o crime organizado. Até agora, 22 foram barrados ou renunciaram e ainda há casos que não foram julgados de forma definitiva.

A ideia é discutir e elaborar uma proposta com mecanismos de monitoramento, análise de riscos e medidas efetivas.

identificar eventuais necessidades de aperfeiçoamento normativo e institucional relacionadas à matéria, apresentando propostas às instâncias competentes;

elaborar relatório conclusivo contendo diagnóstico, propostas de atuação e recomendações destinadas ao fortalecimento da capacidade institucional da Justiça Eleitoral para prevenir e enfrentar os impactos da criminalidade organizada sobre o processo eleitoral.

Fachada do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral — Foto: Luiz Roberto/Secom/TSE

A resolução também lista entre os objetivos do grupo avaliar a necessidade de aperfeiçoamento dos sistemas e da tecnologia de apoio às investigações e aos processos judiciais , além de propor ações de capacitação e intercâmbio de experiências destinadas a magistrados e servidores da Justiça Eleitoral, com enfoque na criminalidade organizada.

O grupo terá quatro meses para realizar estudos sobre o impacto da criminalidade organizada no processo eleitoral , avaliando riscos de interferência, financiamento ilícito de campanhas, infiltração em estruturas políticas e administrativas, coação de eleitores, intimidação de candidatos e restrições ao livre exercício da atividade político-eleitoral.

articles.title: Patinetes elétricos compartilhados começam a circular em Uberlândia | G1
articles.standfirst: Serviço fica disponível a partir de sexta-feira (27), com previsão de 500 equipamentos na primeira etapa. Aluguel será feito por aplicativo e terá cobrança por minuto utilizado.
articles.summary: Patinetes elétricos em Uberlândia serão operados pela Go JET em fase experimental; confira as regras de uso, valores e locais de estacionamento na região Central.
articles.body:
Patinetes compartilhados passama circular em Uberlândia — Foto: Go JET/Divulgação

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Patinetes elétricos compartilhados começam a circular em Uberlândia na sexta-feira (27). O serviço poderá ser usado para deslocamentos curtos, com aluguel por aplicativo e estacionamento em pontos virtuais espalhados pela cidade. A primeira etapa da implantação prevê 500 equipamentos na região Central.

O valor do aluguel será a partir de R$ 0,39 por minuto, além de uma taxa de R$ 0,99 por desbloqueio do patinete . O lançamento do serviço será às 11h, na Praça José Mota, no cruzamento das avenidas Rondon Pacheco e Francisco Galassi, na região do Centro de Tecelagem.

A operação será feita pela empresa Go JET, autorizada pela Prefeitura a implantar o sistema em caráter experimental. O período inicial será de 90 dias, com possibilidade de prorrogação por mais 90, após avaliação da Secretaria Municipal de Trânsito e Transportes (Settran).

Para usar o serviço, o cidadão deve baixar o aplicativo Go JET, disponível gratuitamente para iOS e Android.

A implantação será dividida em três etapas e a ampliação não será automática. Cada fase depende da avaliação e aprovação da Settran.

1ª etapa: região Central, com previsão de 500 patinetes

2ª etapa: expansão para os setores Leste e Oeste, com até 750 equipamentos

3ª etapa: expansão para as regiões Sul e Norte, com até mil patinetes

Entre os locais previstos para estacionamento estão trechos da avenida Rondon Pacheco, a região dos campi Santa Mônica e da Faculdade de Educação Física e Fisioterapia (Faefi) da Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU), além das avenidas Liberdade e Presidente Médici.

Segundo a Prefeitura, na sexta-feira (27), alguns desses pontos já contarão com os equipamentos.

O uso dos equipamentos é permitido apenas para pessoas com 18 anos ou mais, mediante cadastro e verificação de idade na plataforma.

A velocidade máxima será de 20 km/h, com possibilidade de limites menores em determinados locais, conforme determinação da Settran.

Os patinetes terão monitoramento por geolocalização, que permitirá delimitar as áreas autorizadas para circulação e estacionamento.

É proibido deixar os equipamentos em locais que atrapalhem a passagem de pedestres, como calçadas, rampas de acessibilidade, travessias e outros espaços públicos.

O patinete estacionado irregularmente deverá ser recolhido pela empresa em até 60 minutos após ser comunicada ou identificar a ocorrência.

A operadora também será responsável pela manutenção dos equipamentos, orientação dos usuários, atendimento e contratação de seguros para acidentes pessoais e danos a terceiros.

Segundo a Prefeitura de Uberlândia, as regras de circulação, estacionamento, segurança e responsabilidade referente ao uso dos patinetes compartilhados são da Go JET, em conformidade com a legislação de trânsito vigente.

Nos Termos e Condições de Locação do Go JET, o usuário pode encontrar informações sobre as regras de cobrança e reembolso, penalidades por estacionamento irregular ou seguros e responsabilidades.

A empresa utilizará vias e espaços públicos municipais para a operação, com pontos virtuais de estacionamento.

A Prefeitura acompanhará e fiscalizará o serviço durante o período experimental, que poderá ser interrompido ou ajustado conforme a avaliação de funcionamento e segurança.

Como contrapartida pelo uso dos espaços públicos, a empresa deverá repassar ao município 5% da receita bruta mensal obtida com a operação.

articles.title: Bessent insulted Democrats. Now he needs to make a deal with them.
articles.summary: The Treasury secretary has traded barbs with some of the Democrats he'll need to help avert a fiscal crisis next year.
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has spent nearly two years publicly belittling Democratic lawmakers. Soon, he'll need their help to keep the United States from descending into a fiscal crisis.

The U.S. is on track to hit its $41.1 trillion borrowing limit within weeks of Democrats taking control of Congress, setting up a showdown that could come to a head as early as next summer.

Bessent may have some fences to mend first. The secretary has insulted Sen. Elizabeth Warren 's intelligence, saying the next chair of the Banking Committee "knows even less about foreign exchange markets than she does about banking."

He asked Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, to "maintain some level of dignity" after she asked the chair, Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), to "shut him up" during a hearing. And he accused incoming Senate Finance Chair Ron Wyden 's son of being an associate of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

"My experience with the secretary is — 'easy' is not the first word that comes to mind," Wyden, whose committee has jurisdiction over debt limit action, told reporters earlier this month.

Bessent's history of personal attacks will test whether he can broker a deal between President Donald Trump and Democratic leaders before Treasury runs out of cash to pay the nation's bills. A protracted debt limit standoff, even if it ultimately gets resolved, could rattle bond markets and push up borrowing costs.

Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island, a senior Banking Committee Democrat, was more direct about Bessent's relationship with his party: "I don't think it's very good."

But the Treasury secretary has already signaled he wants to work with Democrats when they take over the House and Senate next year. At a Heritage Foundation event earlier this month, he said he would "try to take something out of the Bill Clinton-Newt Gingrich playbook" in fiscal negotiations with Congress' incoming majority — a nod to the bipartisan budget deals struck in the 1990s between the former Democratic president and Republican speaker.

"Look, people like Bessent because he works hard — and he is MAGA, but he is also respected by CEOs no matter what party they are," a senior Trump administration official granted anonymity to speak candidly said in a statement to POLITICO. "The President gives him big projects, and he gets at it."

A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment.

For decades, action on the debt limit has spurred high-stakes standoffs on Capitol Hill over how to reverse the nation's fiscal trajectory, with the risk of default often becoming a point of leverage in partisan negotiations. Generally speaking, Democrats support "clean" debt ceiling increases while Republicans demand that they be paired with larger concessions around curbing federal spending.

If Democrats don't like what they hear in talks with Bessent or other top Republicans this time around, they have other options for raising the debt limit. They could follow the GOP's example from last year and raise the ceiling through a party-line budget reconciliation package — daring Trump to sign it or risk downgrading the U.S. credit rating and spooking Wall Street investors.

They could also ask Senate Republicans to agree to a last-minute deal to raise the debt limit with a simple-majority vote as they did in 2021 .

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), the incoming Budget chair, described his own relationship with Bessent as "pretty much nonexistent." But taking the gavel, Kaine said, means "the relationship, by necessity, is probably going to get a little more communicative."

Even some Republicans say Bessent has relationship-building to do if he wants to influence policy during the next two years.

"He needs to get here," Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said of Bessent in an interview last week. "Honestly, I think one of the challenges the administration will have is there just hasn't been enough relationship between the Cabinet here and Democratic members of the House and the Senate."

But Lankford praised Bessent as being "very in the details. I think he'd be a good negotiator to be able to carry the president's message."

Despite the public clashes, some Democrats think more highly of Bessent than of many other top Trump officials, said a Democratic lobbyist who works on financial services issues.

"A lot of Democrats view him privately as someone they can work with on certain issues," said the lobbyist, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly.

This isn't the first time the Trump administration has had to raise the debt ceiling under divided government; Trump's first Treasury secretary, Steven Mnuchin, negotiated directly with then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi on a 2019 deal to suspend the limit for two years.

Joe Lavorgna, a former senior counselor to Bessent at Treasury who is now chief economist at SMBC Nikko, predicted a standoff over the debt limit this time around: "There's going to be a lot of brinkmanship and a lot of fighting. I hope I'm wrong, but I don't think it's going to go smoothly."

Bessent will have to contend with lawmakers in both parties who want to use debt limit negotiations as an opportunity to overhaul the whole federal budget process, including potentially triggering debt limit increases and spending caps when Congress adopts a budget.

"There really is a prospect of trying to make our rather feckless budget process more sensible and effective," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said in a recent interview.

Other Democrats now see an opening to demand an end to debt-limit standoffs for good — for instance, Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan Boyle , the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, has a bill aimed at ending high-stakes debt ceiling showdowns by allowing Treasury to suspend the debt limit, subject to a Congressional override.

Warren, meanwhile, hasn't forgotten that Trump endorsed scrapping the debt ceiling in December 2024, just weeks before he returned to office — and that Bessent, during his confirmation hearing last year, told the Massachusetts Democrat that, if Trump "wants to eliminate the debt ceiling," he would work with Congress and the president to make that happen.

"This is one more place where I agree with Donald Trump. We need to put an end to it," Warren told reporters last week.

It's not clear if Trump still holds this position, or if he will be able to maintain it amid pressure from conservatives to fight efforts to raise the debt ceiling without major concessions. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Longtime congressional deficit hawks also note that many of the fiscal constraints enacted during past debt limit negotiations were overridden in subsequent years — including "pay-as-you-go" triggers for across-the-board cuts enacted in 2010 to make sure the federal government doesn't spend more than it brings in. This could harden their resolve to fight efforts to pass a "clean" debt ceiling increase next year.

"The disappointing thing is everything we've ever done in the past has been abrogated and ignored," Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said in an interview, adding that he also feared Bessent could broker a debt limit deal that includes an agreement on new funding totals that would substantially increase spending next year.

Sen. Rick Scott said GOP fiscal hawks will be urging Bessent to steer debt limit talks toward achieving "fiscal sanity." Asked how much room Bessent would have to negotiate a deal, the Florida Republican pointed back to the secretary's boss.

"He's a hard worker. But ultimately, Trump is actually the one who's negotiating," Scott said. "There's only one president."

While the United States has never defaulted on its debt, top economists have projected that reaching that point would spark a severe recession, costing the economy millions of jobs and wiping out trillions of dollars in household wealth.

That kind of economic turmoil would be a stain on the legacies of congressional leaders, as well as Bessent and Trump.

"We have to do it. And he should be very concerned," Reed said of Bessent. "If they don't raise the debt limit, they're going to have serious financial problems. … This has to be done. I hope he realizes that."

articles.title: Sean Hannity has outlasted Fox rivals. Now he’s eyeing the GOP’s future.
articles.summary: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. – America had swung to the left with a historic rebuke of President Donald Trump, and Sean Hannity wished it was still Nov. 5, 2024. In...
articles.body:
Sean Hannity has outlasted Fox rivals. Now he’s eyeing the GOP’s future.

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. – America had swung to the left with a historic rebuke of President Donald Trump, and Sean Hannity wished it was still Nov. 5, 2024.

Instead of another Trump win, it was Nov. 3, 2026, and Hannity, the face of Fox News since the network's inception 30 years ago, could only joke on air: He wasn't going to flee to Ireland like a certain Trump nemesis now that Democrats had won the biggest congressional landslide in 50 years. Besides, he was only 10 days removed from his splashy Mar-a-Lago wedding weekend festivities to Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt – and now was not the time for a honeymoon or a move.

"Hatred is a hell of a motivator," he concludes of the Democratic turnout.

Since Election Day, this kingmaker for the political right has been trying to reason on air that midterms can be predictable for presidents with dominant personalities, but nothing about Texas going blue is cyclical. While the MAGA fever appears to have broken, there is a silver lining for Hannity: The Hannity Primary to help decide the next Republican presidential nominee is about to begin.

Nov. 7, 2028, has been on Hannity's mind. He plans to interview every Republican presidential candidate on his show, guessing that Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) would be among the favorites. There are three questions he will pose to the contenders:

Will the coalition be broad enough so that person can win?

These are the same questions he asked of Trump during "very long, late-night, deep conversations about every topic imaginable" in the early days of his long-shot 2016 campaign. "I was very straight with him," Hannity says from the brown leather chair on his podcast set, "and said, 'If you don't convince me, I'm not going to vote for you, and I will not support you.' Period."

When Hannity liked the answers, he became Trump's most influential and dependable ally in the mainstream media in the decade that reshaped American politics. Republicans muscling their way to the 2028 nomination don't necessarily need Trump. What they really need is the support of Hannity and what he did for Trump.

"You could be the perfect conservative, but if you don't have the ability to win a race, why would I support you?" he asks, adding that Trump was "the right man in the right place at the right time with the right personality."

At 64, Hannity is many things to the generations who've heard and seen him rise from Long Island kid and college dropout to one of the most prominent and most hated conservative voices on radio and TV over the last three decades.

To his allies, he is the standard-bearer of conservative talk radio whose shows on TV and radio remain essential to understanding this extended MAGA era of American life. Even at a time when Fox's leading ratings have taken a sizable hit - including a 27 percent drop in total viewers last month compared to October 2025 - Hannity, the longest-running cable news host in history, consistently ranks among the top-five cable news programs nationwide in both viewers and in the coveted 25-54 demographic. Forbes has estimated his annual salary from Fox at about $25 million.

To his critics, Hannity is despised for using his vast media empire to peddle poisonous propaganda in defense of Trump and his agenda.

In 2017, he heavily promoted the false conspiracy surrounding the murder of Democratic National Committee staffer Seth Rich, despite no evidence linking Rich as WikiLeaks' source of hacked DNC emails. Fox News eventually retracted the story and agreed to pay millions to Rich's family to settle out of court. Asked to comment, a Fox spokeswoman sent the network's statement from the time that it hoped the settlement "enables Mr. and Mrs. Rich to find a small degree of peace and solace moving forward."

Hannity had also repeatedly amplified Trump's false claim that his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden was rigged. Before Fox News settled the defamation lawsuit brought by Dominion Voting Systems for $787.5 million, Hannity said in a sworn deposition that he did not believe Trump's false claim that the election was stolen "for one second." A Fox spokeswoman said that Hannity testified he had aired the claims to allow for proof to emerge.

"Him promoting the Seth Rich conspiracy theory was really disgusting, and illustrated his place in the MAGA era," says Oliver Darcy, a veteran media reporter and the founder of the Status newsletter. Nicole Hemmer, a political historian at Vanderbilt University, and the author of "Messengers of the Right: Conservative Media and the Transformation of American Politics," adds that Hannity survived both incidents when other hosts wouldn't because "he's made Fox News much more money than they ended up paying."

"The audience has really developed a taste for these deep conspiracies, and he was serving it up," she says.

Hannity prefers to point to a list of stories that he claims he was right about when other mainstream journalists dismissed him, from the innocence of Richard Jewell at the 1996 Olympics to the investigation of Russian interference in the 2016 election.

"We've been vindicated more times than I can count," he claims, defiantly.

To watch Hannity on TV is to see a relentless, right-wing messenger and tastemaker whose opinions you know you'll never be able to change. Even when he might be wrong, he knows he's right.

As the last remaining prime-time anchor from Fox News's original 1996 lineup, Hannity has survived an abysmal beginning to his career, low ratings, advertiser boycotts and flashier opinion hosts who've come and gone - Glenn Beck, Bill O'Reilly, Tucker Carlson.

"Sean is very good about people and their needs, their understanding of politics and culture, and he moved with that," says Fox News host Laura Ingraham, a longtime friend who credits Hannity for urging her to join the network. "Sean is both just a really good analyst and entertainer because you have to engage people in these topics."

Hannity's steadfast support of Trump has continued in the president's second term, such as on a recent episode of his Fox show when scrolling graphics touted Trump's alleged "Top Accomplishments."

"We talk on the phone all the time," Hannity says, but insists he can keep his personal relationship with the president separate from his professional one.

Critics say there's almost no daylight whatsoever between Trump and Hannity. But ESPN host Stephen A. Smith has a different take on what his close friend has meant to Trump: "I don't think Trump would have become president without Sean."

"If Sean Hannity is in your corner, you won't find someone more doggedly in support of you than him," Smith continues. "You're going to have to go through him and a ton of brick walls he puts up to get to his friends. Because come hell and high water, he's gonna do everything that he possibly can do to protect the people that he supports and he cares about. It's who he is, for better or worse."

"I'll let other people make that judgment," Hannity says, adding of Trump, "We still have a personal relationship. I'll put it that way."

Now, as Fox News celebrates its 30th anniversary this fall, Hannity is reflective about his life and career, namely his place in media, the Trump era, and his future. Would he entertain leaving Fox when Trump exits the White House more than two years from now? Of course not. If you haven't been paying attention for the last 30 years, Hannity is not going anywhere - and suspects that his monologues would continue in his car once he eventually signs off.

"It would not be a good look if I stopped at a light - 'Who is that crazy guy talking to himself? Is that Sean Hannity?'" he says. "But I'm not planning on talking to myself anytime soon."

Today he is talking to Rahm Emanuel, former White House chief of staff, former Chicago mayor, current Democratic presidential aspirant.

"We can be nice and ease our way into open warfare," says Emanuel, before the cameras start rolling for the taping of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity," or "we can go nuclear."

On the podcast set in West Palm Beach with a refined man-cave aesthetic featuring brown liquor, a neon sign, pool table, samurai swords and a signed Matthew Tkachuk Olympic hockey jersey, Hannity flips through a thick stack of stapled, printed-out notes before the taping begins. It's how he arms himself to go to battle with Emanuel for the next two hours. They joust about the Obama years, the Chicago years, the ambassador to Japan years - and whether Emanuel should run for president.

Ambassador is a bulls--- [title], let's be honest.

You have your memory, and then I have the facts.

Stepping into Hannity's world is a road game for Emanuel, but he gets his shots in, too. "As always," he says of Hannity, "you tell half the story." After the pair is finished dropping verbal bombs on each other's heads, they pose for an I-guess-we-will-take-a-photo-together photo to commemorate the marathon taping. Hannity is relieved but not tired.

"I know Rahm's a smart guy," the host acknowledges afterward, "but there was no way I was coming into this interview today not prepared."

Sean Patrick Hannity was not always this prepared, not when he was a bigmouthed kid with strong opinions who smoked cigarettes in between innings of Little League games he was pitching. He loved his parents for eventually instilling a strong work ethic in him, even if his father beat him with a belt whenever he got sideways. A two-time college dropout, he worked in restaurants, construction and started his own house-painting business in Rhode Island, before moving to Santa Barbara, California. It was there, in his late 20s, that he began hosting a talk-radio show at KSCB-FM, the volunteer radio station for the University of California at Santa Barbara.

He discovered that talking in front of a microphone was what he wanted to do for the rest of his life. He also discovered what could get you fired: Less than a year in, he was sacked for casting doubts about the AIDS epidemic and telling a lesbian mother that he felt bad for her child. He later admitted his comments were "ignorant and embarrassing."

Hannity used his firing as self-promotion, framing himself as "the most talked about college radio host in America" and a budding conservative shock jock. He worked at radio stations across the South until Roger Ailes came calling to pluck Hannity from obscurity and put him on the ground floor of a new cable network called Fox News. Hannity was terrible - truly terrible. When he was paired in a nightly talking heads duel with liberal co-host Alan Colmes for "Hannity & Colmes" in 1996, the first review was so rough that he remembers it verbatim three decades later.

Alan Colmes looks funereal; Sean Hannity has a bad haircut and has no business being on TV.

"I asked management once why they didn't fire me," he says. "They said, 'Well, nobody was watching, and we knew you were a broadcaster and that you would get it.'"

The higher-ups were right. Hannity became the cable-news authority on what the conservative base was feeling and thinking, Ingraham says.

"The appeal of him is he is the comfort watch: You know exactly what you're getting almost all the time with him," Hemmer says. Darcy adds, "Some people come up fast and burn out really fast, but Sean is just there ."

The highs were high when Hannity went solo with his own show in 2009; the same viewers who had tuned in to watch Hannity steamroll Colmes now wanted Hannity to steamroll everyone, even if he wasn't always the funniest or most photogenic personality on the network.

But his audience began to shrink in the early 2010s, and moving his show from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m. hurt even more. The tea party movement had fizzled, and the GOP lacked a true leader. Reports were also swirling that Fox would change its direction, and that Hannity was on his way out after the Rich debacle sparked advertiser boycotts.

Then, something happened: Trump, the real estate mogul and "The Apprentice" host had, in Hannity's eyes, become a fun character who would be great for the political contest because of his outspokenness and enthusiasm. That is, if the billionaire ever decided to run for president. When Trump did, Hannity and Ingraham became the first and most emphatic at Fox to put their full weight behind him in 2016.

"I was on the night before [the election] with him, and he looked at me and said, 'Hell, we better be right about this or else we have to change our names and move to South America,'" Ingraham recalls.

"Donald Trump would have been fine on his own," says Dan Bongino, the radio host and former FBI deputy director, "but I think he would tell you himself that having Sean onboard early was definitely helpful in the start of what became this MAGA movement, which I believe a lot of people hope even outlasts President Trump."

Hannity's style is a throwback to the conservative talk-radio ecosystem of the '90s where he was created: fast-talking and confrontational, passionate and provocative, and above all, hyper-partisan. Compared to segments featuring liberal guests and Democrats, which can feel like an anything-goes barroom brawl, his interviews with Trump officials and Republicans are largely seen as casual catchups with friends.

Which is why in the wake of a brutal and fleeting inaugural press briefing, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia retreated to Hannity's show, where she believed she would find a soft landing and a chance to reset. But when the segment began, Hannity grilled her about her legal education and why the briefing was so short. When the interview concluded, Zacharia was left wondering what the hell had just happened. She was fired the next day, lasting just five days in the job. "The overt hostility was unexpected considering I was President Trump's hand-selected press secretary," Zacharia says to The Washington Post of Hannity. "Even a hostile anchor would likely not have treated me with such animosity."

When asked about the segment, Hannity maintains it was not "a sanctioned hit by the president," saying, "I was not trying to attack her in any way. But I knew as the interview was going on, I'm like, 'Uh oh, you're not putting this to rest at all,'" he says. "Her next briefing, if she had one, would have been a disaster, in my humble opinion. And I don't wish that on anybody."

Hannity says he's at a point in his life where he's no longer upset about conservative or mainstream media members sniping at him, but that doesn't mean he's going to forget, either.

There's Ben Shapiro and Glenn Beck, who "spent three years of their life kicking the crap out of me on their radio shows, and saying I'm not a real conservative." There's Tucker Carlson, who told NPR in September about how Hannity had fallen into a ratings trap and "doing the same show every night because it worked three years ago … don't do that."

"I'm not going to take advice from a guy who got fired from NPR, CNN, MSNBC and Fox News," Hannity says of Carlson, noting that they got along when he was at Fox. "I wish him the best in his career, but if I wanted career advice, he would not be the guy to go to." (Carlson did not respond to an interview request.)

He has other ways to spend his time. Krav Maga workouts. Florida Panthers hockey. And, most importantly, Earnhardt, 50, who he had been quietly dating when Vanity Fair broke news of the relationship in 2020.

The couple married in October in Palm Beach, Florida, where Hannity moved himself and his studio permanently in 2024. It was his second, her third, sealed with a lavish series of celebrations attended by a guest list thick with boldface names from the administration and Fox News. Lee Greenwood performed. The bride and groom both wore white.

The weekend began with a Mar-a-Lago pre-wedding reception that Trump and first lady Melania Trump attended.

The president did not offer any marriage advice, Hannity says, still hoarse three days after the festivities. And Trump also didn't pipe up again with the advice he had given Rupert Murdoch years before:

Mr. Murdoch, why do you even pay him? He'll do it for free .

"I'm looking at him like, 'Can you please be quiet? You don't have to tell him,'" the host recalls. "I don't get much friend time with him anymore. I can easily bifurcate my professional role with him and my personal role with him. Not everyone has that, I understand, and there are critics of that, and I'm fine with that, too.

"But I'm not being dishonest with my audience, at all, about any of it."

It seems spot-on for a man who follows the news obsessively and texts his producer story and monologue ideas at all hours of the day and night. Soon, one of those ideas will be the beginning of the Hannity Primary, and the 2028 Republican presidential candidates will go on the show to try to win arguably the most important Republican blessing on prime-time TV.

"I felt Donald Trump could win," he says, "and I was not wrong."

articles.title: Iowa braces for Army’s lead blast
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Army set for lead blast ▪ Thanksgiving travel faces challenges ▪ Giuliani receives highest civilian honor ▪ Administration freezes Virginia district funds Programming note: Morning Report will return on Monday. Happy Thanksgiving! Iowans are bracing for the Army to detonate nearly five tons of unstable lead-based explosives this morning. Federal officials…
articles.body:
▪ Giuliani receives highest civilian honor

▪ Administration freezes Virginia district funds

Programming note: Morning Report will return on Monday. Happy Thanksgiving!

Iowans are bracing for the Army to detonate nearly five tons of unstable lead-based explosives this morning. Federal officials urged residents near the blast site to evacuate and released maps showing the lead dust plume could reach even northern Missouri.

The Army plans to carry out the controlled detonation at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at around 10 a.m. EST but, in an advisory, said that “a more precise time will be communicated after evaluating changing weather patterns and waiting for the safest possible conditions.” The Army said it would update its plume maps hourly in the six hours before the blast.

By Tuesday, some residents were already sealing their windows and doors, and businesses in nearby West Point were preparing to close, The Associated Press reported. Tape and masks were available outside government buildings.

The Army urged residents in the evacuation zone — a 5-mile cone extending southwest of the detonation site — to evacuate beginning yesterday. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is offering transportation, food, water and hotel rooms through Friday, and officials said the residents will get a call when it’s safe to return.

Those who live outside the evacuation zone are encouraged to shelter in place, close windows and doors, and turn off fans that draw in outside air. Sean Kaufman , a senior federal health official, warned that pregnant women , young children and people with chronic illness are particularly at risk and urged them to heed officials’ advice to evacuate.

Army officials also said they planned to use sand, water and foam to limit how much lead escapes into the air and that government officials will “return immediately to conduct post-detonation sampling with results published when available.”

Federal and state agriculture officials estimate that about 350 farms could be affected along the projected path, Iowa Public Radio reported. Iowa officials urged farmers to bring livestock indoors and protect their feed and water supplies. The state is working with federal officials to test forage and livestock after the blast.

A federal appeals court cleared the way for the blast on Monday after two Iowa environmental groups challenged the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) emergency permit, arguing in part that the EPA gave too little public notice and failed to adequately address how lead dust could spread.

The Army issued a public advisory on Nov. 15, five days before the blast was originally scheduled, though it says it discovered the deteriorating explosives in March. The Army says the material is now at risk of spontaneously exploding on its own.

President Trump on Monday said the operation should go ahead only if the court cleared it and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) agreed. Sand fired back, saying the administration must make the decision and explain to Iowans why it considers the blast the best option.

Outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) backed the Army’s plan yesterday , saying she took its warning seriously about an uncontrolled explosion. The state opened its emergency operations center last week to coordinate with federal officials.

Some public officials criticized the way the government approached the planning and called for greater transparency, but few were willing to outwardly call on the Army to take a different approach.

Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst (R) said the Army began discussing detonation with some communities months ago, but “critical details, including the potential lead plume and how far it could reach, were not part of those initial conversations.”

She also said many locals were not included in those talks and only learned about the planned detonation last week.

“At a time when trust in our institutions is already low, the military owes the people it serves more transparency, not less,” she said. “These materials should never have been allowed to get to this point, and Iowans are right to be frustrated.”

Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) took it a step further: “The Army is detonating 9,700 lbs. of toxic lead tomorrow, just a day before Thanksgiving, and they are telling us this is the only possible route. I don’t buy it. They must take every possible precaution to protect families tomorrow. And then we need answers about how this was allowed to happen.

▪ The Hill : Army set to detonate lead munitions in Iowa: What to know.

▪ The New York Times : See How the Army Plans to Blow Up Five Tons of Toxic Lead Compounds in Iowa.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly apologized to his employees and said he was in daily therapy during his first all-hands meeting since he was reinstated. He also played down President Trump’s role in his return to the company.

Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) conceded his Senate race to Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D) almost a week after the race was called by major news outlets. The results of the final outstanding Senate race this cycle were certified on Monday, and Peltola won by a margin of a little more than 4 points.

The Pentagon has had discussions with Ford about supplying highly capable vehicles that would give the military options to lower costs and improve reliability for soldiers, a spokesperson confirmed to The Hill . The talks also include working with space systems contractor Revolution Space to build advanced satellites.

Confetti fills the air as the Tom Turkey float makes its way down Central Park West during the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York on Nov. 27, 2025. (Frank Franklin, Associated Press file)

TRAVEL TROUBLES: A coastal storm is threatening to disrupt Thanksgiving travel this week as millions head out for the holiday, with heavy rain expected across parts of the southeast today, and strong wind and rain expected to move into the mid-Atlantic and Northeast tomorrow.

The National Weather Service expects the greatest risk of coastal flooding from North Carolina’s northern Outer Banks to New Jersey, with a flood watch in effect from Thursday afternoon through late Thursday night. In Washington, D.C., forecasters expect wind gusts of up to 45 mph on Thanksgiving Day.

A high wind watch is in effect for the New York City area from late Thursday morning into early Friday, with the potential for wind gusts of up to 60 mph. NBC News forecasts wind gusts could reach 40 mph by 10 a.m. tomorrow, which has sparked concerns that the giant balloons could be grounded during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

AAA projects 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home this week through Monday, a slight dip from last year’s record. Nearly 73 million Americans are expected to drive, with the heaviest traffic expected between noon and 7 p.m. today, according to transportation analytics firm INRIX.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) expects nearly 418,000 flights — the most in 16 years — over the holiday period.

Gas prices have fallen to an eight-month low of a national average of around $3.61, but prices still remain $0.54 higher than Thanksgiving last year, according to AAA .

▪ The Hill : Trump cautions holiday travelers about ‘antiquated’ air traffic control system.

▪ The Weather Channel : Thanksgiving week travel delays: storms on both coasts.

▪ The Associated Press : How to make holiday travel less of an expensive hassle.

HIGHEST HONOR: Trump awarded former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom , the nation’s highest honor, for his “lifetime of service to the American people.”

Giuliani, Trump’s longtime ally and former personal attorney, rose to national fame as “America’s mayor” in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attack in New York City and became known for his “tough on crime” approach to city governance. In recent years, he helped lead the president’s charge to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, eventually leading to his disbarment in New York and Washington.

Giuliani said he is “honored and humbled” to receive the award , adding , “I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together.”

▪ Politico : Zohran Mamdani joins cities in suing to block Trump’s housing rule.

SOARING CONFIDENCE: Consumer confidence rose to its highest level in nearly two years, as election uncertainty eased and gas prices continued to decline.

The Conference Board said yesterday that its index rose to 103.3 from 91.9 in October, the second straight increase since hitting a 12-year low in September. The 11.4-point jump exceeded expectations, with economists telling The Wall Street Journal that they expected a slight bump to 92.2.

The news reflects partisan divisions. Confidence rose sharply for Democrats and independents but declined modestly for Republicans.

▪ The Hill : Gas prices easing but still squeezing Americans.

The president holds executive time and policy meetings from Florida. He is also expected to meet with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang watches as President Trump points from stage at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press)

CHIP CONTROL: Trump’s successful campaign to pressure Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO of the company has had the unintended consequence of reigniting efforts on Capitol Hill to pass stronger export controls on chip manufacturing.

Brendan Steinhauser , a Republican strategist and CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI, told The Hill’s Julia Manchester and Mallory Wilson that “The momentum has clearly shifted.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee who likely will become the panel’s chair in January, said Huang’s reinstatement “only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law.”

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), who also sits on the Banking panel, echoed Warren’s point in a Bloomberg interview yesterday.

“This also absolutely reinforces what I and a number of other members of the Senate have been saying, which is we need more legislation to restrict the export of these most advanced chips,” McCormick told the outlet.

“I think this gives additional momentum to those legislative efforts,” he added.

Lawmakers who want tougher export controls are focused on making additions to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a defense policy bill that has been approved every year by Congress for decades.

Lawmakers are expected to make a push to pass it in the lame-duck session, though they face various challenges. Steinhauser put the chances of it passing in a bipartisan manner through the NDAA at 50-50 “or maybe higher.”

The bills would allow Congress to block advanced AI chip exports to U.S. foreign adversaries, block the sale of essential chipmaking tools to countries of concern, and would require AI chips subject to export controls to have a “location verification mechanism,” respectively.

▪ The Hill : How much did Trump stand to make from Huang return?

▪ The Hill : Todd Blanche grilled over handling of Huang affair, Nvidia chip exports.

Education Secretary Linda McMahon testifies during a Senate Committee on Appropriations subcommittee hearing on Capitol Hill, April 28, 2026, in Washington. (Mariam Zuhaib, Associated Press)

FUNDING FREEZE : The Department of Education directed Virginia to withhold federal funds this week from Albemarle County Public Schools after the district discovered it had failed to complete the required child abuse and neglect registry checks for 524 employees hired over the past three years.

The district closed schools to its students from Nov. 19 through the end of Thanksgiving break to work through the backlog, but the Education Department still announced on Monday that it would place the Virginia Department of Education on “high-risk status for its apparent failure to enforce state and federal laws” and withhold federal funds from the district “until it can demonstrate that these failures have been corrected.”

“A school division needing to shutter the doors of its schools to ensure that students are not forced to interact with sexual predators is an unfathomable failure of the school division and state leaders,” Education Secretary Linda McMahon said.

All 524 employees had undergone fingerprint-based criminal background checks when they were hired, but the district failed to submit their information for the separate Child Protective Services registry check, according to the district’s acting superintendent, Chandra Hayes .

Hayes responded to the federal announcement saying the district had cleared 519 of the 524 hires through the registry check as of Monday. The other five applications were returned because of clerical errors, but the district said it was correcting and resubmitting them. Hayes expects schools to reopen on Nov. 30.

“These issues are real, and fixing them takes time, commitment and accountability. Our students and families deserve a division that meets every obligation it has to them. That is the work in front of us, and it is the work I am committed to,” Hayes said.

The Education Department said several district employees already face investigations or indictments over alleged sexual misconduct involving students, but it did not specify whether those employees were among the 524 new hires. The federal agency said it would move to suspend and bar from federal programs any employee who has been indicted or who it considers complicit in the district’s failures.

▪ ABC13 : Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) criticizes high-risk status for Virginia schools.

The lame duck Congress can give Indian Country long overdue truth and healing , New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland (D) and Nikki Santos write in The Hill.

It’s up to the Supreme Court to save academic freedom in the US , Austin Sarat writes in The Hill.

Robert De Niro and Jane Fonda (Chris Pizzello and Scott A Garfitt, Associated Press)

And finally … Nearly three dozen celebrities and political donors, including actors Jane Fonda and Robert De Niro , released a letter yesterday endorsing Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) in his bid to unseat Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) when Democrats takes the majority in January.

The 35 signatories — who said they contributed or helped raise about $23 million for Democratic congressional candidates this cycle — argued that Americans voted for change when they delivered a historic blue wave earlier this month.

The public figures who signed the letter include comedian Chelsea Handler , actor Marisa Tomei , television personality Padma Lakshmi and former BlackRock executive Morris Pearl , The New York Times reported .

articles.title: Universities must help solve our severe cyber-readiness labor shortage
articles.summary: Employers advertised more than 514,000 cyber positions and could find qualified candidates for only about three-quarters of them.
articles.body:
In September 1941, three months before Pearl Harbor, Rear Adm. Leigh Noyes, the Navy’s director of communications, wrote to Ada Comstock, the president of Radcliffe College. He needed codebreakers. Could she help him find students suited to the work?

Similar requests reached other women’s colleges that fall. Those who were chosen took a secret correspondence course in cryptanalysis, and by the summer of 1942 the first of them had reported for duty in Washington.

When Noyes sent that letter, the Navy had a few hundred codebreakers. By war’s end, the Army and Navy together had 20,000. About 11,000 were women — many recruited straight from campuses, others from classrooms where they had been teaching. It worked because the request came early, while there was still time to train, and because the colleges delivered.

Presidents from roughly 200 colleges and universities in the NSA’s cyber education network convened this month at National Defense University with defense and government leaders to discuss the workforce the nation needs. Noyes’s letter is worth remembering, because what the Navy grasped in 1941 still holds true today. Equipment can be bought in a budget cycle; expertise cannot. The men and women who get the most out of a new system take years to develop, and in our experience the military rarely has enough of them.

We believe cyberspace is where that shortage matters most today, and recent events punctuate that point. Roughly 225,000 people make up the Department of Defense’s cyber workforce. They defend the networks behind every military operation, conduct offensive cyber operations, and provide critical intelligence. The Pentagon must compete for each of them with banks, hospitals, utilities and technology companies.

The reality is that today’s supply of such expertise falls far short. In a recent year employers advertised more than 514,000 cyber positions and could find qualified candidates for only about three-quarters of them.

Why should a hiring statistic concern anyone thinking about readiness? Because recent conflicts have shown cyber operations, electronic warfare, as well as autonomous systems being used right alongside conventional forces, and every one of them runs on technical skill.

The military is good at growing quickly when it must. It can call up reserves and speed up production lines. Nobody, however, has found a way to expedite developing talent that can defend an industrial control system or find intruders in networks built to hide them. That takes years of schooling, followed by more years of training and supervised work. The specialists who will be needed in a crisis must be in the pipeline long before that crisis starts.

The country does not have to build much that is new. The National Security Agency manages the National Centers of Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity — more than 500 colleges and universities plus six senior military colleges that educate students in cyber defense, research and cyber operations to a defined standard. Add community colleges and research universities, and a program is within reach of students in every state. These institutions can do more than award degrees. They can retrain people already serving, put students to work on real mission problems, and carry out research the department needs.

Further, the challenge today is not a lack of talent at colleges and universities already, but the critical need for it now. Our national security workforce is getting old, with a median age of 47 and nearly 14 percent retirement-eligible. Equally challenging, our workforce today is underrepresented in the career fields that matter most: AI, data science, machine learning, and quantum. Nowhere is this more evident today than with AI, where most of expertise is in the private sector.

What drives universities to build new curricula is outside demand. Over the last decade, we have seen the demand for cybersecurity experts outpace the availability of qualified graduates. What helps incentivize and build university programs is their proximity and association with government agencies that do this kind of work. The University of Texas at San Antonio, as just one example, was on the leading edge of cyber schooling owing to their close association with the Air Force Cyber Command and NSA.

What schools have lacked is clear direction from the defense establishment. Tell a dean that the nation needs more cyber talent, and you have given them very little to work with. Sit down with them and work through which roles must be filled, which skills they call for and at what level of proficiency, and they can build a curriculum around the answer.

None of this is new for the U.S. Less than a year after Sputnik, a Republican president and a Democratic Congress passed the National Defense Education Act, on the premise that the nation’s security depended on the trained abilities of its young people.

We keep coming back to Noyes’s letter. When he wrote it, he could not have known what the students he was asking for would be called on to do. Neither could the students themselves. What the Navy understood was that it would need capable people for problems it could not yet describe.

The same is true now. We cannot say what the next threat will look like or where it will come from; in our experience it is rarely the one we planned for. Equipment is built for the threats we can foresee. Well-trained people are how a nation handles the ones it cannot. The young Americans who could do that work are in classrooms across the country today.

Gen. Stanley McChrystal (Ret.) is the former commander of U.S. and international forces in Afghanistan and of Joint Special Operations Command. He is founder and CEO of McChrystal Group. Gen. Paul M. Nakasone (Ret.) is the former commander of U.S. Cyber Command and director of the National Security Agency. Adm. William H. McRaven (Ret.) is the former commander of U.S. Special Operations Command and former chancellor of the University of Texas system.

articles.title: The FAA wants $50 billion, but it last built a control center in 1969. Is this a good deal?
articles.summary: Shouldn’t we worry that a bigger check, handed to the same flawed FAA structure, will just buy the same results at a higher price?
articles.body:
Ten days ago, a four-hour nationwide ground stop led to more than 18,000 flight cancellations . By Tuesday the Trump administration was asking Congress for $50.1 billion .

Yes, fix the problem, absolutely. But a blank check for an agency with this track record is a bad bet. The FAA last built an en route air traffic control center in 1969 , the same year Apollo 11 put two men on the moon . Congress should impose conditions before it writes the check.

Start with the cause of the problem, which nobody agrees on. The Transportation Department blames outdated legacy equipment. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says a newly installed router set off intermittent communications and radar problems at 17 of the 22 centers that direct high-altitude traffic. He also claims that 68 earlier installations of the same routers went fine . The FAA says the root cause is still unclear .

Aging equipment and a new router are two different explanations for one outage. I wouldn’t sign off on a family office’s $50,000 expense line, never mind $50 billion, with so much uncertainty.

The price tag has also moved faster than the evidence. In 2025 the department said it needed another $20 billion on top of the $12.5 billion Congress had appropriated. In September, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford testified that $10 billion more would do it . Duffy then sent lawmakers a $30.1 billion request on Nov. 12 . By the night of the outage, he wanted $50 billion .

Only $10.1 billion of the $50.1 billion goes to the digital architecture and controller safety tools. The rest covers airport grants, terminals, five new centers and up to 140 towers. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee, said some of it is “not safety related.”

Then there’s the money Congress has already sent. The department says all $12.5 billion is allocated and on track to be spent by 2028. House Appropriations Democrats Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) and James Clyburn (D-S.C.) say that $9.1 billion in previously approved funding remains unspent, and they point to an Office of Management and Budget apportionment holding more than $5 billion of the reconciliation money until Oct. 1, 2027.

You can’t call something an emergency and park the cash in the same breath. I don’t mean to treat Democrats’ accounting as gospel, but the administration owes Congress an answer on that one.

As an expert witness in fiduciary cases, I often hear questions about who was accountable, and what did they verify before the money moved. In private credit, nobody wires full loans on day one. Lenders release funds against milestones. Borrowers who miss milestones hear about it.

To be completely fair, this problem long predates the Trump administration. The Government Accountability Office found in 2024 that 51 of the FAA’s 138 air traffic control systems were unsustainable . It added that the agency had been slow to modernize its most critical systems. Duffy says 20 to 30 years of piecemeal funding got us here, and he has a point. But shouldn’t we worry that a bigger check, handed to the same structure, will just buy the same results at a higher price?

Two administrations, two sets of priorities. In November 2021, Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told reporters about highways “built for the purpose of dividing a white and a Black neighborhood.” Even though his claim was dubious , he used it to make racial equity a public priority at the department, including at least $1 billion in the infrastructure law to reconnect divided communities. That same law gave air traffic control $5 billion over five years .

Duffy has put the system first, and his pitch has grown from a 2025 modernization plan to $30.1 billion on Nov. 12 to $50.1 billion five days later. Results matter more than priorities, let alone dollars thrown at the problem. So far, neither administration has delivered a finished system.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) says Congress will take up the request in the lame-duck session , which is how a $50 billion item gets buried in a year-end bill. Give it its own bill and its own vote, so every member has to own the result.

So attach conditions. Release the money in tranches tied to public milestones. Use fixed-price contracts with penalties for missing dates. Name one accountable executive who answers to Congress when a date slips. Spend down the unspent balance before a new dollar moves. Require a public root-cause report on the Nov. 13 outage before router installations resume. Sunlight is the best disinfectant, and a quarterly scorecard is cheap.

Then look north. Canada transferred its air traffic control system to a private nonprofit, NAV Canada, on Nov. 1, 1996, for 1.5 billion Canadian dollars . It runs mainly on user charges rather than government appropriations .

Cato’s Chris Edwards describes the result as “one of the safest systems in the world,” even if the safety data comes from the company’s own reporting. Duffy’s 2025 modernization plan didn’t contemplate privatization , and the Canadian model carries risks of its own. But it still deserves a hearing before we spend $50 billion rebuilding the old structure.

Thanksgiving is this week. Apollo 11 landed on the moon in 1969, the same year the FAA built its newest en route center. We’ve been to the moon, and we are aiming for Mars. Meanwhile, we are still flying like it’s 1969.

Congress can change that, but only if it demands a finish line before it signs the check.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management. He writes about issues in finance, constitutional law, national security, human nature, and public policy.

articles.title: What to expect once the new Democratic House majority gets its oversight powers
articles.summary: Expect “legitimate legislative purpose” to be burned into your brain over the next two years. As Democrats take control of Congress, the party is careening toward a battle with the executive branch over who has the power to check the other. Tension is already ratcheting up, raising questions about just how far Democrats will be able…
articles.body:
Expect “legitimate legislative purpose” to be burned into your brain over the next two years.

As Democrats take control of Congress, the party is careening toward a battle with the executive branch over who has the power to check the other.

Tension is already ratcheting up, raising questions about just how far Democrats will be able to go in their oversight of everything from the president’s crypto interests to investigations of key administration officials.

Yes, we’re talking about the Teapot Dome scandal.

The corruption stain that plagued the Harding administration made its way up to the Supreme Court in 1927. A Senate committee had subpoenaed the brother of the attorney general over concerns the official was failing to investigate the corruption scandal.

In McGrain v. Daugherty , the Supreme Court ruled that Congress has the power to compel witnesses to testify. The court reasoned that it is essential to ensure lawmakers have the necessary information to legislate.

“Experience has taught that mere requests for such information often are unavailing, and also that information which is volunteered is not always accurate or complete; so some means of compulsion are essential to obtain what is needed,” Justice Willis Van Devanter wrote for the court at the time.

“All this was true before and when the Constitution was framed and adopted.”

That’s the good news for Democrats. Expect them to cite McGrain plenty over the next two years.

Republicans will, meanwhile, look to Trump v. Mazars , when the modern Supreme Court put limits on congressional oversight powers.

At the time, Democrats were focused on Trump’s personal financial records during his first term.

In a 7-2 decision authored by Chief Justice John Roberts , the court said requests for the president’s personal information raise special separation of powers concerns. He laid out a four-factor balancing test for courts to consider:

Necessity: Does lawmakers’ asserted purpose warrant involving the president’s papers?

Scope: Is the subpoena broader than reasonably necessary?

Evidence: Do lawmakers have evidence that establishes the subpoena will advance a valid purpose?

Presidential burden: How will the subpoena encumber the president?

That’ll be the make-or-break standard, at least for Democrats’ efforts to get personal records concerning Trump.

Already, Democrats have a laundry list of subjects they’ve signaled they’ll probe. Here are a few:

Trump family business dealings, including Jared Kushner ‘s role in a private equity firm while spearheading U.S. diplomacy efforts in various international conflicts

World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency venture Trump launched with his sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump in 2024

Corporate donors to the White House ballroom, no-bid contracts and potential conflicts of interest

The tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, including the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti , during Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota

The administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files

Dive deeper: Our colleagues Judy Kurtz and Niall Stanage break down the investigations likely coming, and how Democrats can balance their oversight priorities with legislative ones.

The White House is going on the offense, using preemptive legal threats and internal policy shifts in an effort to stymie Democrats’ investigations before they’ve had a chance to get started.

Days after incoming House Oversight Chair Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) told the administration to “lawyer up,” White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter warning that the probes could cross the line into “blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz has also sent threatening letters to several top Senate Democrats telling them to preserve documents, despite having virtually no jurisdiction over activities in D.C. or the legislative branch.

And just last week, President Trump issued an executive order that directs federal contractors to notify the White House of any “pending or future congressional request” and requires them to abide by its instructions on the “withholding of communications” deemed protected by executive privilege — the scope of which has also been expanded in recent months.

“The doctrine of executive privilege, which the Supreme Court has recognized is inextricably rooted in the separation of powers under the Constitution, protects confidential executive branch information from disclosure,” the order states. “Protecting this information from unauthorized disclosure, including to members of the Congress, is vital to the functioning of the executive branch.”

Experts say the president’s directive leaves third-party contractors caught in the middle, potentially exposing them to legal risks if they defy a congressional inquiry.

“In trying to bolster its defenses against the forthcoming wave of oversight, the administration is once again treating its business partners as expendable—no more than political footballs,” Jessica Tillipman , the associate dean for Government Procurement Law Studies at George Washington University Law School, wrote in an op-ed for GovExec . “It is placing them in the impossible position of choosing between an existential risk to their business today and contempt proceedings tomorrow.”

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams. Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

Proxy voting: The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled that a COVID-era rule that allowed House members to vote by proxy violated the Constitution’s Quorum Clause , blocking enforcement against Texas of a provision of Democrats’ $1.7 trillion spending package that protects workplace accommodations for pregnant people.

A Thanksgiving-eve blast: The Army’s controlled detonation of nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at an ammunitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, is going ahead on Wednesday after the 8 th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals denied an emergency request from two environmental groups to halt it while their broader legal challenge over the EPA permit continues.

Arch construction blocked, again: U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema has blocked the Trump administration from moving forward with construction on a 250-foot arch at Memorial Circle near Arlington National Cemetery, the second federal judge to halt the plans. The Justice Department quickly appealed to the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals

East Potomac stays open: The golf course at East Potomac Park will remain open to the public through at least mid-December after U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes extended a temporary restraining order that blocks the National Park Service from closing the property while she considers a longer injunction.

Onward for one of Trump’s defamation suits : Trump’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and publisher Penguin Random House can proceed , U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday ruled. He dismissed claims challenging statements in an article about the president’s former television show “The Apprentice,” however.

Gobble gobble : Two West Virginia turkeys named Freedom and Feathers will live out their days at Texas A&M as the lucky recipients of a presidential pardon, sparing them from the Thanksgiving dinner table. It officially became an annual tradition during former President George H. W. Bush’s administration in 1989. Watch this year’s ceremony at the White House .

Gorsuch talks civic engagement: Need some entertainment for your Thanksgiving travel? Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch and Janie Nitze, co-authors of the new children’s book “Heroes of 1776,” joined George Mason University’s Access to Excellence podcast last week for a conversation on the importance of civic engagement in the modern era. Watch or listen here.

Enjoy your turkey tomorrow, but then, get ready, because the Supreme Court is coming in hot next week.

The justices’ December session kicks off Monday and is jam-packed with several arguments that will thrust the justices into the culture wars, all as they mull a series of hot-button requests to take up new cases.

Here’s what you need to know before they take the bench:

Background: The Supreme Court will decide the fate of bans on AR-15s and “assault weapons” passed in blue states and cities across the country. It’s the latest case implicating the 6-3 conservative majority’s expanded Second Amendment test that requires gun restrictions to be consistent with the nation’s historical tradition. The court has held that “dangerous and unusual” weapons can be regulated, but gun rights groups say the bans go too far.

What we’re watching for: The impact of a New York Times report that the late Justice Antonin Scalia misquoted the “dangerous and unusual” phrase when cementing the standard in a seminal 2008 Second Amendment decision. Some legal conservatives dispute the notion and say Scalia’s citation was proper.

Background: Parents are challenging changes to Washington state law that instruct youth shelters to not notify parents when they receive their runaway child, if the child is seeking gender-affirming care. The plaintiffs say it violates their parental rights. A judge found they didn’t have legal standing to sue. The Supreme Court is hearing their case only to review standing issue, though it’s being closely watched by many major groups for what it could bode for the broader parental rights issue.

What we’re watching for: If the justices reveal any more of their thinking on their March ruling that California was likely acting unconstitutionally by blocking teachers from disclosing to parents when their child changes their name or pronouns in class. That was just an emergency ruling, so the vote lineup wasn’t all public. The Dec. 7 argument could provide more clues.

Background: The case centers on whether Arizona can require applicants to submit documentary proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote with a state form. Lower courts have ruled that the challenged laws are preempted by the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 and violate a 2018 consent decree between the secretary of state and the League of United Latin American Citizens. The court is also set to decide whether the state can implement a program to remove noncitizens from its voter rolls.

What we’re watching for: Trump has previously touted a nationwide proof-of-citizenship law as his No. 1 legislative priority, so watch how he and others in his administration react to the arguments. At least three federal judges have already struck down an executive order that would implement the requirement for all voter registrations, ruling that the president overstepped his authority.

Background: As part of its aggressive immigration crackdown, the Trump administration has removed migrants to countries where they have no ties, called third-country deportations. The administration says its policy is focused on deporting violent criminals. It has signed agreements with countries across the globe, largely in Africa, to take in these deportees. A federal judge ruled the policy doesn’t give the individuals enough opportunity to raise claims they’ll face torture or persecution. The Supreme Court has allowed the deportations to resume until it issues its ruling.

What we’re watching for: How the Trump administration handles an unusual offer from the justices. The Supreme Court hears cases only to decide specific questions. In agreeing to take up this case, the justices unusually added an open-ended prompt: “Such other questions that the Government determines are appropriate for the proper disposition of the case.” Watch to see where Solicitor General D. John Sauer takes that — since he apparently has some more free rein here.

As those arguments unfold, the justices are filling out their docket for the end of the term.

They are entering their final sprint, as mid-January marks the unofficial scheduling cutoff where cases start getting assigned to next term.

Remember, the Supreme Court chooses which cases it hears and turns away the vast majority. Only about 2 percent of requests are taken up.

We expect the justices will wade through hundreds of requests during two closed-door meetings during the December session. Here are some we have our eyes on:

Transgender troops ban: President Trump wants the justices to greenlight his ban on transgender troops serving in the military. An appeals court has ruled the Pentagon can only enforce it against new recruits. Previously, the Supreme Court handed Trump a win in the battle, but that was an emergency ruling that is only technically temporary. The case is now back for a final ruling.

E. Jean Carroll: The Supreme Court already declined to take up Trump’s appeal of writer E. Jean Carroll’s $5 million sexual abuse lawsuit. The president is now appealing Carroll’s second trial win, where she won another $83.3 million over defamation claims. The president has the support of the Justice Department, which claims Trump shouldn’t be on the hook for defamation damages because Carroll’s lawsuit concerns things Trump said while president.

US Attorneys: The Justice Department’s unusual maneuver to install unconfirmed prosecutors atop U.S. attorney’s offices and keep them there beyond the allowed 120 days is facing its first test at the high court. The justices are weighing whether to review challenges involving Sigal Chattah in Nevada and John Sarcone III in the Northern District of New York, who were disqualified from some criminal cases after lower courts held that they were serving unlawfully. The Trump administration claims the rulings “risk chaos” for future transitions of administrations, while opponents urge the court not to “wade through such murky waters.”

Horseracing : A long-running battle with massive stakes for the horseracing industry is coming to a head. In 2020, Congress overhauled a patchwork of state regulations to implement national anti-doping standards. It faces a challenge claiming the law unconstitutionally handed over power to a private group to create those standards. Everyone involved — states, industry players, the private group, even the Trump administration — says it’s time for the justices to step in.

The court could also soon begin releasing opinions in cases argued earlier this term.

Though the start of the term had plenty of excitement — including a massive lawsuit against the climate industry by Boulder, Colo. — don’t expect the big ones quite so soon.

The justices typically start with a unanimous opinion and decisions in low-profile cases where there is broad agreement.

Groups suing over grant cuts at the U.S. Agency for International Development are due to submit a scheduling proposal alongside the government for the next stage of the legal fight.

Federal courts are closed for Thanksgiving.

Most federal courts are closed or in recess for the Thanksgiving holiday.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia , a case deciding whether public school and university employees can sue their employers for sex discrimination under Title IX, and Wassily v. Blanche , a case examining whether someone whose asylum status was terminated can still apply for a green card.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Jouppi v. Alaska , which asks whether Alaska violated a man’s constitutional rights by seizing his plane after a passenger flew in alcohol to a dry village.

A federal judge in Massachusetts will hold a hearing to consider several motions in a lawsuit challenging a May 2025 memo that authorized federal immigration officers to make arrests without judicial warrants, including whether the case should be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
