articles.title: Democrats made gains with male voters — creators can help us keep them
articles.summary: If Democrats want to sustain their gains with male voters, they can’t treat creators as a novelty to be deployed every two or four years.
articles.body:
In 2008, I helped elect Barack Obama president during a moment when digital media was transforming American politics. Nearly two decades later, another transformation is underway — and the 2026 midterms may have offered Democrats their clearest indication yet of how to take advantage of it.

The thesis I pondered on Nov. 4, after what can only be described as a heady, thrilling night for me and my team, was: If President Trump won in 2024 because of a shift amongst white, male, non-college-educated men, did those same voters help deliver Democrats’ victories on Tuesday? And what will it take to keep them in 2028?

According to NBC News exit polling , roughly 67 percent of young men voted for Democrats in the 2026 midterms. Even more remarkable, Trump had won young white men by a commanding 28 points in 2024 . Just two years later, that same demographic favored Democrats by over 21 points — a 49-point swing toward Democrats.

It’s easy to lay all the blame on Trump’s well-padded shoulders, but this victory was about more than his failures. It’s also worth paying attention to the growing success of left-leaning creators who are beginning to compete with MAGA in the very online spaces that helped propel Trump to victory in 2024.

Creators like ItsLuke , Ohh that’s RICH , Mr. Global , Amanda Nelson and Lisandra Vazquez are taking advantage of a huge gap in the creator marketplace — a void left by the crumbling online ecosystem that helped galvanize Trump’s second victory.

The right-wing creator ecosystem that helped power Trump’s 2024 victory is showing signs of fragmentation. Some of its biggest personalities have broken with Trump, while others are struggling to maintain the audiences and influence they once commanded. That creates an opening for progressive voices willing to engage audiences, particularly men, on their own terms.

Sure, it’s very hard to win unless or until the opponent makes one unforced error after another. However, one development Democrats should build on is collaboration between candidates and the growing swath of left-leaning creators and independent media outlets that are getting compelling messages in front of audiences that traditional political media often struggle to reach.

At my organization, our creator network grew to 17.6 million combined followers in less than a year, generating more than 70 million short-form views. And over 70 percent of our audience is male — the very demographic Democrats have struggled to reach.

I don’t mean rage bait and cheap clicks. I mean domain experts with huge audiences with smart, well-produced clips that break down tough and sometimes wonky concepts into something funny, moving and — at the very least — memorable.

To keep this momentum going, this collaboration can’t stop. If Democrats want to sustain their gains with male voters, they can’t treat creators as a novelty to be deployed every two or four years. Congressional members and their staff have to treat us like they would any media professional or organization.

Include creators and independent media on media blasts and do more interviews with those creators. Come to our events and speak directly to audiences. Invite creators to in-person pressers and events and fund creators and independent media to compete with the right

In reality, Democrats are the only adults in the room right now, the nation’s sole leaders with the moral compass to end the illegal war in Iran. Our leadership can end the tariffs and lower prices. This next crop of congressional Dems will address housing costs, insurance access, affordability and so much more.

We will do so through awkward congressional mechanisms and processes like budget reconciliation, potentially veto overrides, oversight committees and hearings that could lead to indictments.

Do nerds like me digest that stuff? Oh, all day and twice on Sunday. But to most folks, it’s boring, dense and indecipherable. But a creator? They can make it funny and scream it from the rooftops.

Not to undersell our massive achievement (we all deserve the victory lap), but beating a president with a 30 percent approval was the easy part. We know democrats have a better vision for our country’s future. We just need leaders who partner with a burgeoning information ecosystem to sell that vision.

Democrats have an opportunity to make our online ecosystem even bigger than the one MAGA once enjoyed, but the work has to continue into and beyond 2028. The 2026 election may have given Democrats an opening with male voters. What they do between now and 2028 will determine whether they keep it.

Tim Fullerton is the co-founder and CEO of Find Out Media , the first-ever creator-led media company. A longtime digital media executive and political strategist, he previously served in the Obama administration, led digital strategy for the State of New York, and co-founded White Dudes for Harris .

articles.title: Plane crash off the coast of Mississippi kills 6, including 2 children
articles.summary: Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi Tuesday, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.
articles.body:
(AP) — Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi Tuesday, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.

Divers found their bodies in the fuselage of the aircraft after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore, according to officials. There were four adults and two boys, ages 8 and 10, on board, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile reported at about 3:45 p.m. that it lost contact with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. Responders spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.

The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.

Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard Sector Mobile Search and Rescue Mission Coordinator, called the situation heartbreaking.

“While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families,” he said in a statement.

The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board, which will investigate the crash, said Tuesday they were aware of it.

Earlier this month, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in south Florida, killing all nine people on board. The terrifying crash was captured on video recorded by people inside their cars.

articles.summary: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who is vying for another term as Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) chair, says Democrats could expand their Senate majority to 60 seats in the 2028 election and would back their incumbents in general-election races, including Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.). Gillibrand told NBC News that growing the Senate Democratic majority to…
articles.body:
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who is vying for another term as Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) chair, says Democrats could expand their Senate majority to 60 seats in the 2028 election and would back their incumbents in general-election races, including Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.).

Gillibrand told NBC News that growing the Senate Democratic majority to 60 seats in 2028 is “definitely possible,” and she said Democrats have “easy targets” in North Carolina and Wisconsin.

Democrats will control 56 seats in 2027 after beating Republican incumbents in Alaska, Kansas, Maine, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina and flipping GOP-held, open seats in North Carolina and Texas.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Picking up four more Republican seats would give Democrats a filibuster-proof Senate majority, something they could use to pass long-standing priorities, such as increased federal support for healthcare and childcare and new disclosure rules for campaign spending.

“It’s on the table,” Gillibrand told NBC of the prospects of Democrats controlling 60 seats in 2029. “There’s some easy targets that I’m very excited about — obviously, Wisconsin and North Carolina,” where Republican Sens. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) and Ted Budd (R-N.C.) will face reelection.

She argued the blue wave that helped Democrats pick up nine Senate seats in this month’s midterm election could last another two years.

“I would also suggest any state that was in play last cycle is in play this cycle. Waves tend to be two cycles long, and this is a very large blue tsunami,” she said.

Gillibrand says the Senate Democratic campaign arm would defend all incumbents in the November 2028 general election, including Fetterman, a centrist who has clashed with progressive activists over U.S. support for Israel.

Gillibrand said she is assuming Fetterman will run for another term until he announces other plans.

“So far, we assume he is. And we are going to win Pennsylvania.”

Asked whether she would support Fetterman in the general election if he manages to win a Democratic primary, Gillibrand said she would.

“We support our nominees,” she said. “We support all our Democratic nominees.”

Pennsylvania will be one of several swing states that Senate Republicans will target in 2028, along with Arizona, where Sen. Mark Kelly (D) will be up for reelection; Georgia, where Sen. Raphael Warnock (D) will be up for reelection; and Nevada, where Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D) will face voters.

Kelly and Warnock are viewed as potential presidential candidates in 2028, but Gillibrand is expecting them to run for reelection to the Senate, at least for now.

“I assume so, but we’ll find this out over the course of the next few months,” she told NBC News.

articles.title: America’s farmers deserve our thanks for all the gifts they give us each day
articles.summary: As Thanksgiving nears, we should be grateful for farmers and ranchers who will supply more than 5 billion pounds of turkey this year for American tables.
articles.body: As we approach Thanksgiving, I am mindful of the many blessings we enjoy as Americans and grateful to the men and women who make them possible. That especially includes our farmers and ranchers, whose hard work produces an abundant harvest year in and year out. In mid-November, I saw America’s unrivaled agricultural heritage up close once again while visiting Dean Gaps Farms in West Virginia, one of America’s many family-owned and operated turkey farms. For more than a decade, owners Scott and Becky Rightsell have continued a proud family tradition of raising turkeys for Americans to serve at their Thanksgiving tables. Their efforts are now being recognized in a very special way, as two of their turkeys were chosen as this year’s Presidential Flock. That means these birds traveled from Pendleton County, W.Va., all the way to the White House, where President Donald Trump pardoned them in a Rose Garden ceremony. THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION This time-honored tradition does more than spare two turkeys from ending up on someone’s Thanksgiving plate. It also shines a spotlight on our patriot turkey farmers, who raise the finest turkeys in the world and are expected to supply more than 5 billion pounds of turkey this year. In 2025 alone, American turkey production was valued at $5.58 billion — and naturally, consumer demand is only going up. While Thanksgiving is the Super Bowl for American turkey farmers, this magnificent bird is a delicious and affordable source of protein and nutrients no matter the season. Chock-full of immune-boosting vitamins like iron, zinc, potassium and chromium, turkey also supports healthy bone development and heart health. And this year, Americans can be thankful that the average price of a 16-pound turkey is about 15% lower than at this time of year in 2023. THANKSGIVING DINNER KITS: 7 GROCERY CHAINS OFFERING HOLIDAY MEALS FOR UNDER $70 From Day One, Trump has made clear that supporting America’s farmers and fostering a healthier future go hand in hand. To that end, earlier this year, we flipped the food pyramid and released new dietary guidelines that encourage more whole, nutrient-dense proteins. It’s all possible because of our incredible farmers, who dedicate their lives to maintaining the world’s healthiest and most abundant food supply. Beyond stewarding the land and raising livestock, our farmers cultivate and renew the values that make our way of life possible. Walk onto a farm, and you will find a commitment to faith, family and the frontier spirit that have characterized this week’s holiday from the start. BROOKE ROLLINS, DR. BEN CARSON: WE ARE PUTTING REAL FOOD BACK ON SCHOOL LUNCH TRAYS Like those present at the first Thanksgiving in 1621 in Plymouth, Mass., our farmers and ranchers have endured innumerable hardships throughout our nation’s 250-year history. Yet no matter the challenge, their unyielding faith and courage have seen them through and preserved our freedom. As I love to say, every American is important, but it’s the farmers and ranchers who are important to every American. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In his 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation, President Abraham Lincoln observed that our nation’s blessings are so abundant that we are prone to forgetting their original source. But God’s goodness and the grit and the sacrifice of our farmers and ranchers must never be taken for granted. That’s why it is indeed "fit and proper" — in Lincoln’s words — to pause and take stock of the many good gifts in our lives and those responsible for them. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So, between watching football and gathering with family and friends over a home-cooked meal, be sure to say an extra prayer of thanksgiving for the 1.2% of Americans who keep the rest of us fueled, clothed and fed. And to all our ag producers out there, know that the Trump administration will never stop fighting to protect your way of life. America’s future depends on it. articles.title: The Supreme Court is about to take a closer look at Trump’s immigration agenda
articles.summary: Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across...
articles.body:
Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump's immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president's asylum ban , his vast expansion of mandatory detention of migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with dubious human rights records .

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer's blockbuster decision upholding birthright citizenship , the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are "indispensable" to its overall immigration crackdown.

"In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law," said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. "These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular."

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June allowed Trump to end a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang's assertion that the court will find Trump's immigration policies illegal.

"If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name," she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration's immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan vowed to "rip ICE apart." New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker, told CBS that Democrats would "put an end to Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine."

But Republicans have already frontloaded funding for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House chief of staff — a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

"It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature," said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. "Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court."

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president's program.

"Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned," Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

"Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term," he predicted, "I think it's doing the same kind of cleanup."

The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump's push to remove certain migrants to countries other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such "third country" removals in cases when a migrant's home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants' rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the "third country," even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won't be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket, three times allowed the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration's decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration's ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump's first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump's asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration's top appellate attorney, warned the court of a "vicious cycle" that encouraged "illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would 'be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.'"

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the "most important and effective" policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, "threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half."

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm's way.

"These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades," said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

"If the court validates the policies," he said, "it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation's commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms."

articles.title: Army detonates nearly 5 tons of lead azide at Iowa ammunition plant
articles.summary: Two explosions were heard near the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday as the U.S. Army detonated 68 barrels of degraded lead azide — a move officials said was necessary to prevent a spontaneous blast.
articles.body: After multiple delays and a federal court intervention, the U.S. Army has detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Two explosions could be heard in the vicinity of the site at around 9 a.m. local time (10 a.m. ET), according to a video feed. Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley said in a press conference after the explosion that "all the lead azide barrels were definitively removed," adding that there were no secondary explosions, notable dust kick-outs or infrastructure damage. "I believe, absolutely, that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," said Shirley, the commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command. US ARMY MAKES PREPARATIONS AHEAD OF LEAD AZIDE STOCKPILE DETONATION IN IOWA As of 12 p.m. ET, none of the EPA's four live air monitors in the expected plume path have detected any lead in their readings. A senior official within the Trump administration told Fox News that the planned explosion "exceeded all expectations" and that "maximum mitigation" was achieved. That was followed up by a short Truth Social post from President Donald Trump himself, in which he said early reports showed mitigation efforts had been successful. About 15 minutes after the explosion was heard, Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe confirmed that it had taken place. Updated Army maps had projected the blast's plume could drift southwest into the northeastern corner of Kehoe's state. "Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained," Kehoe wrote in a social media post. CONTROLLED IOWA MUNITIONS DETONATION BETTER THAN ‘WORST-CASE SCENARIO,’ ACTING ARMY SECRETARY SAYS Ahead of the blast, residents and environmental advocates had warned that detonating the bomb-making materials at the plant risked blanketing the surrounding community in toxic lead dust. To prevent this, the Army built extensive barriers and deployed specialized gels to absorb the fallout. Maj. Gen. Shirley also credited aqueous foam barriers with helping to contain the blast. After the detonation, FEMA said that residents within 20 miles of the blast site who have not evacuated "should continue to shelter in place" and follow EPA safety guidance. FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton told Fox News there was a "sigh of relief" at the Army's command center following the explosion, which he said was likely effective at containing lead particles. "From what we see now, it doesn't appear that there's a big lead plume that was in the projection models," Hamilton said, adding that the Army's mitigation efforts to contain the blast "were very, very successful." US ARMY TO PROCEED WITH IOWA DETONATION OF DEGRADED BOMB MATERIALS: ‘A CONSENSUS DECISION’ Hamilton said that in the coming days and weeks, various federal agencies will be taking air and soil samples, while officials with the Department of Agriculture will visit nearby farms to carry out impact assessments. Rob Sand, Iowa's Democratic governor-elect, echoed what federal officials have said so far about lead dispersal being limited and thanked those on the ground who worked to make sure the detonation was "as safe as possible." "The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," Sand added. "Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared. There must be immediate transparency to understand how and why this situation became what it did. And any Iowans who have been impacted in any way must be taken care of fully, right away." Officials with the Army and other federal agencies had agreed that a controlled detonation of the 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly volatile explosive material, was safer and far preferable than a spontaneous explosion. Such a blast, officials said, was possible at any moment because the lead azide had crystallized. The crystals are extremely sensitive to heat, shock and friction, and officials warned that freezing temperatures — like those that hit Middletown on Wednesday — could further destabilize the material and trigger an explosion. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP ATF Director Robert Cekada said the lead azide was first brought to the munitions plant in Middletown at some point in 2009, right around the time the U.S. military was beginning to phase out the combustible material due to its extreme volatility. The Army discovered that the lead azide had begun to crystallize during a routine inspection in March, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle has said. The Army initially considered hiring a private firm to neutralize the explosives using chemicals, as well as options for thermal treatment or relocation. However, officials determined that opening the unstable barrels to add chemicals risked triggering an immediate explosion, leading them to pursue a controlled detonation instead. On Nov. 13, the EPA granted an emergency permit authorizing a detonation through February 11, 2027. After the Army set a date for Nov. 20, the Iowa Environmental Council and the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club sued the EPA, which put the detonation plans on hold. Trump ordered the Army not to proceed without court approval, which it got on Monday, when the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals lifted its stay.

articles.title: Prosecutors drop felony charge from 2020 against incoming House Dem
articles.summary: LaKesha Womack settled a 2019 Budget Car Rental bill for a Toyota Corolla she never returned, allowing prosecutors to drop the felony charge.
articles.body: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255). Nearly two weeks after she was declared the winner in the Nov. 3 election, flipping a Republican-held seat, a North Carolina Democrat settled a 2019 rental car bill for a car she did not return, allowing prosecutors to drop a felony charge. Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer B. Merriweather III, a fellow Democrat, dropped the case that featured a court summons served to Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., at a campaign event Oct. 11, more than six years after the Jan. 14, 2020 summons was secured by prosecutors. Womack said she did not know she was wanted for a felony because she was homeless at the time and not able to receive mail. She paid off the rental car company as part of an agreement last week. DEMOCRAT WHO TOPPLED GOP INCUMBENT WILL HEAD TO COURT ON FELONY CHARGE JUST DAYS AFTER ELECTION UPSET "On November 16, 2026, this office was informed of an agreement reached between Defendant Womack and the rental dealer," Merriweather's DA office wrote in a statement Tuesday. "In the days that followed, we were able to confirm that the victim rental corporation received a sum of money from the Defendant equal to an assessed rental cost from the day the vehicle was deemed overdue until the day it came back into the possession of the victim corporation. "In a subsequent phone call with a prosecutor, representatives for the victim rental corporation said explicitly that the corporation did not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved." Womack first appeared in court on the summons one week after being declared a future U.S. House member, and nearly seven years after the summons was issued. The rental car agreement was from Oct. 11, 2019, according to the district attorney, and the car was seized by local law enforcement on Dec. 4, 2019. Womack said she did not receive the official felony court summons until Oct. 11, 2026 — less than a month before the midterm elections — when an officer personally handed her the paperwork at a campaign event. DEMOCRAT HOUSE CANDIDATE HIT WITH FELONY SUMMONS AT CAMPAIGN EVENT Womack has spoken publicly about being homeless without a permanent mailing address after moving back to Charlotte in 2016 to work on the Hillary Clinton campaign. "I was struggling," she said in an October video posted to Facebook. "I was struggled so bad that there were days that I wanted to end my life – that I did not think I was strong enough to push forward. "At one point, I had a rental car, and I did not return the rental car on time. I did not know that they had filed a case against me, because, again, I was homeless and I had no place to receive mail, so I didn't get any notification about it." She added she was "going to figure out how much money do y'all need" to settle. That happened after her first court appearance, according to the district attorney's office's news release. Fox News Digital reached out to Womack's campaign for comment, but they did not immediately respond. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE Just a week prior, Womack defeated incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., by roughly two points in the race to represent North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District. She had rebuked campaign attack ads from friends of Moore targeting her late in the race, calling "the timing of my court date (one full week after Election Day) especially frustrating" and saying diabetes, an intensive car visit, single motherhood and homelessness contributed to her delinquency. "I have experienced some incredibly difficult chapters in my life, including a serious medical emergency that required hospitalization in intensive care," Womack told WBTV-3 just days before the election. "As a single mother living with type 1 Diabetes, that experience was frightening, overwhelming and life-changing. Like millions of Americans, I learned firsthand how quickly an unexpected medical crisis can disrupt your health, financial stability, and ability to provide for your family." The charge, felony failure to return hired property, stemmed from a 2019 Toyota Corolla with an estimated value of $20,000 that Womack rented from Budget Car Rental on Aug. 27, 2019, according to prosecutors and court records. Womack renewed the agreement twice, with the final rental period beginning Oct. 7, 2019, before local law enforcement recovered the vehicle and returned it to the company Dec. 4, 2019. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Womack’s attorney, Harold Cogdell Jr., told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that his client had been "unaware a criminal summons had issued" for nearly seven years and moved quickly to settle the balance once notified. Cogdell noted that the Corolla was returned undamaged 41 days before the criminal charge was filed. The felony became a central attack line in the closing stretch of the race, with Republican ads warning voters against electing a "felony defendant." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "How is she going to be an advocate for our community when she can't manage her own personal affairs?" Moore's campaign told Fox News Digital last month. "As an attorney for over 30 years, I think everyone should be held to the same standard of justice, and this situation is no different. Free legal advice: When the rental agreement ends, so does your right to keep the car." Fox News Digital's Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'Grave concerns' mount as Army moves to restart DC helicopter training after deadly 2025 crash
articles.summary: Rep. Don Beyer says the Army contacted the FAA to resume helicopter training flights near Washington National Airport, but the FAA says no request arrived.
articles.body: Criticism is mounting among experts concerned with the U.S. Army's "risky" plan to resume helicopter training flights near Washington National Airport following a deadly midair collision in 2025. The Army released a plan and told select members of Congress it wants to restart helicopter test flights near DCA — just a few miles from the Pentagon — as soon as Dec. 1, 2026. Backlash immediately ensued. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., asserted on X he has "grave concerns about the decision to resume training flights before the NTSB’s safety recommendations have been fully implemented." A spokesperson for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Fox News Digital that it "has not received a formal request to resume military helicopter flights around Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA)." "Approval from the agency is required before any training in the area can restart," the spokesperson added. FAA, NTSB INVESTIGATING POSSIBLE VIOLATION OF SAFETY PROTOCOL INVOLVING TRUMP, MARINE ONE A U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with American Airlines Flight 5342 in January 2025, killing all 67 people aboard both aircrafts. The FAA subsequently halted military helicopter training flights in the area in May 2025 after another Black Hawk helicopter flew too close to DCA, forcing air traffic controllers to reroute some commercial flights. In a March 14, 2025, statement the FAA said it was "permanently closing [helicopter] Route 4 between Hains Point and the Wilson Bridge and evaluating alternative helicopter routes as recommended by the NTSB." Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., on Monday wrote in an X post that the Army told his office it had reached out to the FAA regarding its request to resume training flights and is currently "awaiting a response." "Army officials assured my office that no flights will take place unless they are approved by the FAA," Beyer stated. His office did not expand on specific concerns when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday. An anonymous Army spokesperson told Politico on Monday "there is intent to resume flights," acknowledging that the move would require approval from the FAA. TRUMP HELICOPTER’S RADIO WARNINGS WENT UNHEARD BEFORE CLOSE CALL WITH PASSENGER JET, REPORT SAYS The DOT referred Fox News Digital to the FAA when reached for comment. "Members of the investigative team and I were briefed on the Army’s plans to begin the initial phase of a return to helicopter flights to the Pentagon through airspace near DCA as soon as December 1st," NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy told Fox News Digital. "It is our understanding that the FAA has yet to receive a formal request for these flights. We have not seen the Army’s concept of operations and look forward to reviewing it once it is formally submitted to the FAA for evaluation." FAA UNVEILS NEW AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLER HIRING PLAN AFTER CHIEF WARNED SYSTEM WAS ‘CHRONICALLY UNDERSTAFFED’ When reached for comment on Tuesday, the Department of War referred Fox News Digital to the Army. The Army did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. Resuming helicopter training flights near DCA could pose "major" safety concerns, according to Randy Klatt, flight safety officer at the Foundation for Aviation Safety (FAS). "Yes, [there are] major concerns considering that no entity — the airlines, DCA, FAA, or the Army — took any proactive action on the thousands of loss-of-separation incidents that preceded the midair collision. Helicopter Route 4 was a trap as designed, yet it was in use regularly until disaster struck," Klatt told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. "Knowing this does not instill any confidence that the resumption of Army training flights will be done safely and in close coordination with the FAA." "There has been no mention of reopening Helicopter Route 4 but for the above reasons FAS would strongly oppose such an action," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Heritage Foundation senior research fellow and retired U.S. Navy Capt. Brent Sadler warned Fox News Digital that there is little justification to restart training flights "or even routine flights" in the DCA area. "Interference to commercial [air] traffic remains a risk," Sadler explained. "Training flights would be better served in a lower activity area at least from commercial civilian air traffic." "There is little reason to rationalize training flights or even routine flights in proximity to DCA," Sadler continued.

articles.title: Federal grand jury hears evidence in Ilhan Omar investigation, as court records use 3 versions of her name
articles.summary: A federal grand jury in Minnesota is hearing evidence as investigators examine whether Ilhan Omar used a false name or birth date to get U.S. citizenship.
articles.body: A federal grand jury in Minnesota is hearing evidence in the investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., sources told Fox News. Federal prosecutors described the case in newly unsealed court records as a "pre-indictment investigation." It remains unclear what evidence the panel has heard or whether it will return charges. There are at least two active investigations underway, according to sources: One into allegations of immigration fraud and another into Omar's finances. ILHAN OMAR APPEARS CLUELESS ON BASIS FOR FEDERAL PROBES: ‘YOU PROBABLY HAVE MORE DETAILS ON THAT’ Omar has repeatedly denied wrongdoing to Fox News Digital in connection with the investigations, but the investigations remain ongoing, and no official charges have been filed to date. The immigration investigation reportedly originated under then-President Barack Obama, while former President Joe Biden's administration opened the investigation into her finances. In a detail sources say is relevant to the immigration probe, court records use three versions of Omar’s name. Investigators are examining whether she used a false name or birthdate to obtain U.S. citizenship. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE The Justice Department’s Oct. 7 brief identifies her as Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, also known as Ilhan Abdullahi Omar. Both names appear together twice in the unredacted portions of the recently released documents. Separately, the warrant return filed by agents stated that a copy of the search warrant was left with Ilhan Nur Said Elmi Mohamed. The records do not explain the differences. The partial unsealing of materials related to the search of Omar’s Washington, D.C., residence stems from an order by Chief Judge James E. Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia after news organizations sought access. The government had initially secured the sealing of the warrant and related documents in October, arguing that disclosure could lead to subjects fleeing, destruction of evidence or witness intimidation. A magistrate judge agreed there were reasonable grounds for those concerns. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION Prosecutors described the matter as seeking evidence of violations occurring between 1980 and the present. That timeframe extends well before Omar entered Congress and aligns with public reporting on her arrival in the United States in the mid-1990s, sources and court filings indicate. Omar claims she was born Oct. 4, 1982, in Mogadishu, Somalia. That birthdate allowed her to obtain derivative citizenship through her father's naturalization, because she was still a minor. Omar has said her father naturalized in 2000. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS A 1981 birth year would have made her 18 by then, while a 1982 birth year would have made her 17. This 1982 birthdate is now listed in her official congressional biography, the Biographical Directory of the U.S. Congress, House History, Art & Archives, and major reference sources. Before May 2019, numerous sources — including the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, Wikipedia, the BBC and other media profiles — listed her birthdate as Oct. 4, 1981. In May 2019, after she entered Congress, Omar’s staff contacted the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library and other outlets to correct the year to 1982, stating the earlier date was inaccurate, describing it as a correction of an error rather than an intentional alteration. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE PAVES WAY TO UNSEAL ILHAN OMAR SEARCH WARRANT IN BLOW TO TRUMP'S DOJ Originally nominated by Obama, Boasberg's release of redacted documents into the ongoing investigation has come under fire. A central dispute in the unsealed materials involves the Speech or Debate Clause and how the search of Omar’s home was conducted. The magistrate judge required safeguards, allowing Omar at the outset of the search to identify and assert privilege over protected legislative materials before agents reviewed them. ILHAN OMAR RECORDS SHOW JUDGE, DOJ OFFICIALS DEBATING BEFORE RAID OF HOME The Justice Department agreed to that protocol but later pushed back, arguing that the court had applied a different standard in another recent search warrant approved by the same judge involving an unnamed individual who appears similarly situated. In that case, according to DOJ filings, agents searched the person’s devices and two D.C. residences without requiring comparable additional steps. Prosecutors also contended that releasing the judge’s account of the dispute while the underlying records remained sealed would present an incomplete picture, since the government is restricted from discussing what it has uncovered. In an interview with the Fox News Rundown podcast that aired Friday, Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said where there's "smoke" then "there may be fire," particularly if you read between the redacted lines. "The Biden administration started this investigation; the fact that a judge appointed by Barack Obama literally scrutinized the reasons that law enforcement was saying we need to have a look at what is on her phone, what is in her residence," Emmer said. "You can't just say, I wanna go search their house. You have to say we have probable cause to believe that a crime has been committed and this is the substance of what we believe and what we think we may find. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And a judge has to scrutinize that and say, 'Well, oh, okay, I agree in this case. There is enough here. There's enough smoke here that there may be fire. And you have the court's permission to do the investigation that you need to do.'"

articles.title: Troubling side effects of Walz’s signature legislation triggering local outrage as he heads for the exit
articles.summary: A viral clip shows a Minneapolis 911 official telling City Council 41 percent of her staff are out on Minnesota's paid family and medical leave program.
articles.body: Minnesota’s new paid leave law, championed and signed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, is already causing major headaches as public employees take advantage of the program at levels that are straining government services. Eleven months after the law took effect — allowing Minnesota workers up to 12 weeks a year off with partial pay to care for a newborn or a sick family member, and up to 12 weeks to recover from their own serious illness — almost one in four Minneapolis city employees has used the benefit, the Minnesota Star Tribune reported. The outlet reported that the absences are putting a "squeeze" on some departments, including the agency that takes emergency calls in the city. On Tuesday, a clip posted by Alpha News from an October budget presentation to the Minneapolis City Council went viral on social media. In the video, Emergency Communications Center Assistant Director Leticia Cardenas tells the council that 41% of her 911 staff were out on Minnesota’s new Paid Family and Medical Leave program. NEW AUDIT IN WALZ'S BACKYARD EXPOSES MASSIVE FRAUD RISK TIED TO POST-GEORGE FLOYD ACTIVISM The high rate of leave has forced remaining operators to work significant overtime to keep the center staffed around the clock, contributing to a proposed $1.5 million budget increase for the department. Councilmember Linea Palmisano pressed Cardenas on whether new hires can immediately take the paid leave and then quit once it ends. Cardenas confirmed both are allowed under the law as currently written, stating that "upon hire with the city, PFMLA can be utilized by any city employee. And then if they decided they wanted to quit working, they can choose to do that." WALZ'S 'EXIT INTERVIEW' REFLECTING ON HIS TENURE SPARKS LAWMAKER DEBATE ABOUT HIS LEGACY: 'NEVER SERIOUS' Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., was among the Republicans on social media criticizing the program after the clip circulated. "This is the definition of waste and abuse," Emmer posted. "Minnesota needs accountability, not more freebies on the taxpayers’ dime." "This program is working exactly as it was designed," Minnesota Republican state Sen. Michael Holmstrom posted on X. "The fraud is so rampant in Minneapolis, even government employees appear to be in on it," conservative commentator Steve Guest posted on X. Bill Glahn, a policy fellow at the Center of the American Experiment, has warned about the program since its inception. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We have been warning for years that this would be the result," Glahn told Fox News Digital on Wednesday. "In the real world, people respond to incentives. Workers will take advantage of a program with the rules as they are written, rather than how advocates originally sold the program to lawmakers." Glahn added, "Next comes the double-whammy tax increases: first to cover the cost of the leave benefit, next to hire more workers to backfill the missing staff." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Earlier this year, just months after the law took effect, the state's largest nonpartisan business advocacy organization and two Republican state senators raised concerns about the program, Fox News Digital reported. Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office and the Minnesota Department of Employment and Economic Development for comment.

articles.title: Trump officials reportedly at odds over tech titan's comeback as national security concerns linger
articles.summary: Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia after Trump and JD Vance intervened, but federal probes into Megaspeed and alleged chip diversion to China remain ongoing.
articles.body: President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance helped bring Jensen Huang back to the helm of Nvidia — a move that has reportedly exposed divisions within the administration and prompted one expert to warn it is "sending the wrong message." The push to get Huang his job back has reportedly put Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the handling of national-security concerns involving Huang’s relationship with a woman whose alleged ties to Chinese intelligence remain in dispute, as well as questions about advanced U.S. chips reaching China. Vance reportedly worked with Nvidia's board over the weekend to get Huang his job back, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who reportedly warned Trump about intelligence concerning the relationship, took another approach. Rubio has not publicly weighed in on the CEO's reinstatement and his office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The Vice President told CNN on Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche assured him that Huang was not under investigation. "But most importantly, at just, I think, a personal level, we received the assurances that he was not under any significant, he was under no investigation, and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," he said. Vance continued, saying that he didn't think it was appropriate anyone should lose their job "because anonymous sources accuse them of things in the New York Times." The Nvidia saga reveals a "definitively split approach within the administration" toward China, as the company pressed for looser export controls, Max Meizlish of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies told Fox News Digital. TRUMP DEFENDS JENSEN HUANG'S CREDIBILITY, NVIDIA'S FUTURE AFTER BOARD REINSTATED CEO, SAYS 'SEX SELLS' Nvidia said it received assurances from senior officials that Huang's reinstatement posed no national-security risk. But federal investigations were still underway into the Nvidia CEO's affair with a suspected Chinese spy and potential diversion of advanced U.S. chips to China when the president began his push. The decision to reinstate Huang has left Republican lawmakers demanding to know what senior administration officials told Nvidia’s board that led them to reverse course less than two weeks after Huang's resignation. The scrutiny intensified Monday when the Commerce Department added Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company tied to Huang’s former affair partner, to its trade blacklist after months of reported disagreement inside the administration over restricting the firm under investigation for allegedly helping divert Nvidia chips to the CCP. Director of National Intelligence (DNI) Jay Clayton, however, said Sunday that investigations into Megaspeed and executive Alice Huang were ongoing, urging officials to "let that investigation play out" and "gather the facts." Trump said Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the U.S. government had no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct. But when asked Monday night whether Huang had been cleared of national-security concerns or violations of federal law, Blanche declined to say. He argued that the question assumed facts about what the DOJ was investigating and claimed "a lot of thoughtful process by administration officials" went into the decision to back restoring Huang. TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT Meizlish questioned the administration’s commitment to preventing chip diversion and told Fox News Digital that restoring Huang "is clearly sending the wrong message." "The company itself certainly has a lot of questions to answer," he added. Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, is under scrutiny over alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Megaspeed is being investigated over possible diversion of advanced chips to China. Bessent said Nov. 13 that Treasury, the State Department, the Pentagon and the U.S. Trade Representative had "for months" supported adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, but conceded that "Commerce has the pen" to decide whether to take action. Bessent said his deputy had been pushing for action. Prior reporting indicates Commerce officials resisted the move while other administration officials pressed for restrictions. Trump later acknowledged that Lutnick may have delayed action to avoid a "blowup with China." Treasury did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment and Commerce did not respond when asked about reports the department dragged its feet on implementing export controls on Megaspeed. JENSEN HUANG IS BACK. NVIDIA’S BOARD STILL OWES AMERICA ANSWERS Republican lawmakers are pressing for answers about what the administration knew before Nvidia’s board decided to bring Huang back. Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, wrote on X: "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?" Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., called Huang’s reinstatement a "mistake," warning it could "whitewash" unresolved national-security questions. The Republican chairmen of the House committees on Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China said the board’s "brief internal investigation and reinstatement" did not erase the threats and questions they are investigating. Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to appear for transcribed interviews with the committees Dec. 1 and Dec. 2. The congressional scrutiny comes amid separate questions about why it took months to blacklist Megaspeed and whether the controls now in place go far enough. TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS Commerce added Megaspeed and six affiliates to the Entity List Monday, the same day Nvidia announced Huang’s return. The designation requires licenses for covered exports to the companies, with applications subject to a presumption of denial. "Commerce will continue to vigorously enforce export controls, including these new Entity Listings," the department said. It explained the listing makes it unlawful to export U.S.-origin goods, software or technology to Megaspeed, and that advanced SI chips are also barred even when made overseas. The scope of the controls is disputed. Former National Security Council official Chris McGuire criticized Commerce for not applying an entity-specific foreign-produced direct product rule, which can extend U.S. export controls to some foreign-made goods produced with U.S. technology. He said that without it, less advanced AI chips and components made overseas — including Nvidia H20 chips and high-bandwidth memory — could still be shipped to Megaspeed. A Commerce official pushed back on McGuire’s characterization, telling Fox News Digital an entity-specific FDPR was unnecessary because the existing Advanced Computing FDPR already places advanced SI chips destined anywhere in the world under U.S. export controls. NVIDIA SPY CASE EXPOSES HOW FOREIGN AGENTS TARGET AMERICA’S CORPORATE ELITE: 'HE IS COMPROMISED' Commerce’s on-the-record statement similarly said advanced SI chips are barred from Megaspeed even when made overseas. McGuire’s criticism focuses on what he says remains outside those rules, including less advanced chips and components. Meizlish said resellers would still need a license to supply Megaspeed, with applications presumed denied. Applying the entity-specific FDPR, he said, could further restrict the company’s access to foreign-made chips and components. Commerce did not specify whether H20 chips or the other components McGuire cited are covered by the existing rules. The White House maintains that its policy has been consistent, with spokesman Matthew Middleton telling Fox News Digital that "America’s most advanced chips must go to U.S. SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies." A White House official also said Trump has repeatedly ruled out allowing China to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell and Rubin chips, and noted that Megaspeed has been under federal investigation since 2024 and Nvidia placed the company on its internal "no sell" list in June 2025. Commerce said last week that the DOJ later took the lead in the criminal investigation. Neither department has announced charges against Megaspeed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lawmakers are set to question Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer next month about the company’s handling of the controversy and the national-security concerns surrounding his return.

articles.title: How the FAA's new Line Up and Wait rules may — or may not — impact Thanksgiving holiday air travel
articles.summary: The new rules require a dedicated air traffic control supervisor to oversee the runway procedure, which could lead to longer waits at short-staffed airports.
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration imposed new standards for its Line Up and Wait airport policy on Tuesday that, though not a significant change, could affect travelers during the busy holiday travel season.

Line Up and Wait (LUAW) is a procedure that allows planes preparing for departure from busy airports to taxi into position on the runway while they wait to be cleared for takeoff. It's designed to make airport departures more efficient by putting planes in position to take off as soon as airspace has been cleared.

Under the FAA's new policy , airports can still use LUAW, but they must designate a watch supervisor whose sole job is to oversee LUAW operations and whose attention cannot be split by other tasks. The new rules change guidance from saying that airports "should" have a dedicated LUAW supervisor to saying that they "must" have one.

The FAA said the change is intended to "elevate the safety standard" for LUAW operations by "removing ambiguity" about staffing requirements under the old rules.

Will the new rules affect Thanksgiving holiday travel?

The impact of the policy change on passengers comes down to staffing. At airports with enough staff to assign one person exclusively to LUAW, the effect will likely be minimal. But airports that may be short-staffed, a chronic problem in recent years, might be unable to use LUAW. That could mean slightly longer waits on the tarmac in some cases.

Even minor delays caused by the new LUAW policy could be compounded by potential disruptions from the Thanksgiving travel rush , with 417,000 flights expected to depart during the 9-day holiday travel period and stormy weather forecast for both coasts.

The new LUAW rules will also be in place for the December holiday travel season. They are scheduled to expire in June.

Though the new policy represents a relatively minor procedural update, it comes at a time when the FAA is under intense scrutiny following the historically disruptive nationwide ground stop that resulted in the cancellation of 18,000 flights earlier this month.

That outage, plus a series of smaller technical disruptions in the weeks since, has fueled a sense of "outage anxiety" among holiday travelers. In a recent YouGov poll, 72% of respondents said they were concerned about "flight cancellations or significant delays as a result of further disruptions to U.S. air travel" over the holiday travel season. Nearly a third said the ground stop could potentially lead them to alter their travel plans.

The new LUAW rules are not related to the ground stop or other recent disruptions. They were first proposed in early October, more than a month before the ground stop occurred. There were no reports of significant delays related to the new rules on Tuesday, the first day they were in effect and the busiest day of the Thanksgiving travel season.

Congress is debating whether to provide the FAA with billions of dollars in additional funding to upgrade its infrastructure and implement other changes to prevent future outages. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has asked for $50 billion , but even lawmakers who support a funding boost for the FAA say the final price tag could be much smaller.

The debate could affect LUAW operations at the nation's airports, depending on whether Congress approves funding to help them address staffing shortages that may limit their ability to assign someone exclusively to LUAW.

articles.title: Far-left podcaster's 'bottom feeder' remark about Melania Trump draws conservative rebuke
articles.summary: MRC's Curtis Houck blasted podcast hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan after Welch referred to first lady Melania Trump as a "bottom feeder."
articles.body: A far-left podcaster's personal attack on first lady Melania Trump this week drew a sharp conservative rebuke. The "I've Had It" podcast co-hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie "Pumps" Sullivan discussed Melania Trump’s Christmas preparations and public image. Welch acknowledged the first lady’s appearance before criticizing her character. "I give credit where credit’s due. I do think she’s a pretty woman. And, I think she’s a really beautiful woman on the outside," Welch said. "But on the inside, I think she’s just an absolute bottom feeder piece of trash." LIBERAL PODCASTERS TELL TPUSA TO ‘F--- OFF’ AS CHARLIE KIRK BACKLASH COSTS THEM ADVERTISERS The co-hosts of the show are known for their vitriolic attacks against Trump supporters, and they came under fire earlier this month when they laughed at a joke about killing Charlie Kirk again. Sullivan added that the movie and TV series about Melania Trump were "dogs---." Houck responded in a statement to Fox News Digital, criticizing both hosts and defending the first lady. "Sadly, their lives are devoid of joy and substance as it's too clogged with takes that seem like the liberal, elitist media concocted while heavily intoxicated after a post-White House Correspondents Dinner brunch." "The First Lady has more class in her pinky than they seem to have possessed in their lifetimes," he continued. WELCH DOUBLES DOWN ON TPUSA FEUD, CALLS GROUP 'LOSERS' AFTER LAUGHING AT JOKE ABOUT KILLING CHARLIE KIRK AGAIN Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.
