articles.title: Dani Carvajal y su ataque más directo al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez: "¿Algo más queda por corromper?"
articles.standfirst: El lateral del Getafe se pronuncia en su cuenta de Instagram
articles.summary: El lateral del Getafe se pronuncia en su cuenta de Instagram
articles.body: Dani Carvajal ha mostrado una opinión contraria a la gestión de Pedro Sánchez al frente del Gobierno. Es la primera vez que el internacional español y futbolista del Getafe se pronuncia de forma tan directa sobre el líder del PSOE. Para hacerlo, ha empleado su cuenta de Instagram, donde ha subido una noticia sobre un nuevo caso que atañe al Ejecutivo. Según El Español, Leire Díez y el exjefe de gabinete de Sánchez están investigados por cuatro delitos más por supuestas irregularidades en Correos. Dani Carvajal ha publicado este artículo, acompañado de la siguiente pregunta: “¿Algo más queda por corromper?”. Una cuestión directa del que fuera capitán del Real Madrid en plena campaña electoral. Hay que recordar que Carvajal fue uno de los jugadores que compartió la reflexión de Marcos Llorente sobre Óscar Puente y el accidente de Urda. También que, como jugador de la Selección, se hizo muy viral su ‘saludo’ a Pedro Sánchez en la Moncloa después de salir vencedores en la Eurocopa 2024. Aquel frío apretón de manos fue el origen de rumores acerca de la opinión del internacional español sobre la gestión del Gobierno. Eso sí, el jugador de Leganés nunca se había pronunciado en primera persona sobre cuestiones del Ejecutivo, PSOE o Pedro Sánchez. El caso que ha indignado al excapitán madridista guarda relación con la decisión de la magistrada Carmen Valcarce de admitir a trámite la querella interpuesta por Vox en noviembre de 2025. Considera que existen indicios de la posible comisión de delitos de fraude en la contratación pública, prevaricación administrativa, malversación de fondos públicos y tráfico de influencias. Este caso implicaría, principalmente, a Leire Díez, conocida como ‘fontanera del PSOE’, y Juanma Serrano, exjefe de gabinete de Pedro Sánchez, según publica el Español.

articles.title: Why deep pockets weren’t enough to save the GOP in 2026: 'Money is not magic'
articles.summary: Despite a $1.7 billion GOP war chest plus $665.4 million from Trump's MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk's America PAC, Republicans still lost badly in the midterms.
articles.body: Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash. Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns. The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi. Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night. MUSK PICKS HIS FIRST GOP WARRIORS AS A 2026 MONEY SURGE TAKES SHAPE On top of their already significant nine-figure lead, GOP electoral efforts were also buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC — which themselves collected an additional $665.4 million for Republicans to burn through. Despite such a massive financial edge, the GOP suffered one of its worst midterm performances in history, losing Senate seats even in deep red jurisdictions like South Carolina and Mississippi. Still, Capital Research Center President Scott Walter, argues: "Money is not magic." "Democrats should remember that when tempted to curtail political speech with donation limits, and Republicans should remember that when tempted to think more money automatically means more votes," the leader of the right-of-center group told Fox News Digital. "That will be news to those like Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., who thinks billionaires and ‘dark money’ control the cosmos." Walter pointed out, citing data aggregated by OpenSecrets, that the biggest donor in any given election cycle rarely ends up getting what they want out of the American political system. Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets, a nonprofit dedicated to tracking money in politics, told Fox News Digital that, while money certainly moves the needle in elections, its actual impact can be blunted by a variety of factors — many of which were at play during the recent midterms. AI IS SUPERCHARGING POLITICAL AD WARS. BUT VIRAL DOESN’T MEAN VICTORIOUS "​​Certainly, you know, the money makes a difference," said Glavin. "When both sides are engaging in a sort of arms race, right, and they're both spending almost equivalently, then really the effect is lost," he explained. "If you're somebody [who] sees an ad for one candidate, and then it's immediately followed by an ad for another candidate… essentially, you're not moving the needle." In many of the marquee races of Election Day, such as the Senate races in Texas and Michigan, both parties had enough money to saturate the airwaves with their messaging, potentially creating the environment described by Glavin. "This election was very unique," he told Fox News Digital. "What people probably really didn’t see until afterward is there was this significant headwind and voters were feeling a certain way and more ads were not going to change that." SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL Glavin, to support his argument, pointed to the fact that self-funding candidates running in elections often fail to make much headway, serving as evidence for the claim that ludicrous amounts of money don’t automatically equate to political success. One of the most obvious recent examples is former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who spent roughly $1.1 billion of his own money on his 2020 presidential campaign. He won only 55 delegates in the Democratic primaries at an approximate cost of $18 million per delegate. Academics who spoke to Fox News Digital were divided on the impact money has on elections. "Money has diminishing returns," Ray La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told Fox News Digital. "And in [an] election wave environment where the president and his party is overwhelmingly disliked or distrusted, money can do little to save them." JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026 John Sides, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University, meanwhile, pointed Fox News Digital to a 2022 study he and two other academics conducted studying the impact of television advertising on election outcomes. According to their study, there is a relatively direct relationship between ad spending and voter share and, while there is a degree of diminishing returns in elections with very high spending, there is still a marginal impact. Joe Arlinghaus, a Texas-based conservative political strategist, told Fox News Digital that how money is spent matters more than how much of it is spent, an assertion he said could explain why the GOP did so poorly despite its hefty cash advantage. "Most people understand that new technologies get better and better and better as time goes on," he said. "Bugs get worked out. Inferior practitioners get pushed aside. Trial and error leads to better and better practices. This is what has been happening in the Democratic election world." He noted that Republicans have failed to keep up on that front. "I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the big SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," Arlinghaus added. Glavin shared that perspective, noting how "Musk just recently commented about how he may be regretting a little bit all the money he spent." "It's hard to tell how serious he is about that and whether or not he'll just come back again for the next election," he added, speculating that the massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving. THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES One source familiar with Republican politics told Fox News Digital that "advertisements pay for mortgages in Great Falls," a reference to claims that political consultants spend money in ways that make them wealthier, not necessarily in ways that help candidates win. Great Falls is a wealthy suburb of Washington, D.C. While Republicans enjoyed an overall fundraising advantage, largely driven by wealthy large-dollar donors, individual Democratic candidates in high-priority races generally raised more money than their Republican rivals, as was the case in Georgia, Michigan and Texas’s Senate elections, among other contests. Some say this should have been an early warning sign for the GOP that grassroots support was wavering, though others are skeptical of such an assertion. Colin Seeberger, the chief strategy officer at the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal advocacy group, told Fox News Digital that the fundraising advantages enjoyed by individual Democrats were a "reflection of voters' enthusiasm for those individual campaigns." He also said voters had an "overwhelming frustration with the direction of the country and how the president and majorities in Congress … were disconnected from what voters said that they wanted [from] the people of their government." BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS "I'm not sure that the party that raises more definitively has an enthusiasm advantage," Sides, the Vanderbilt professor, said, pointing to past elections where Democrats have secured more donations than the GOP but lost anyway. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Seeberger echoed Arlinghaus’ claim that Republicans may have squandered some of their financial advantage by making poor spending decisions, saying, "When you're spending the majority of those sums to talk about issues that register low on the rankings of what voters say are their priorities, there's going to be limited returns on the impact."

articles.title: Autonomous AI agents are giving everyday hackers ‘nation-state’ firepower, cyber expert reveals
articles.summary: Cybersecurity expert John Walsh of IGEL says AI gives individuals the power to disrupt critical infrastructure once held only by nation-states.
articles.body: While the recent string of headline-grabbing service outages across critical U.S. sectors may not be the result of a coordinated cyberattack, governments and companies across the globe still face a reality in which individuals have the same power to disrupt that was once only held by large nation-states, cybersecurity expert John Walsh explained. "AI and the fact that it enables organizations that wouldn't have, let's say, financial resources that a nation-state might have to really invest in a specific type of attack methodology to go after some specific resource or objective, AI definitely enables them," Walsh, the senior vice president at the Germany-based software company IGEL, told Fox News Digital. Since Microsoft's high-profile service outage on Nov. 12, numerous corporations and government agencies have suffered network-related service disruptions. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for just the second time since 9/11 on Nov. 13, citing a faulty router replacement flooding the telecommunications network. TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS Several other critical industries and sectors, including major U.S. banks and the National Security Agency, have also been hit by major network disruptions in the ensuing days. However, the White House and several prominent cabinet members have repeatedly denied seeing any evidence that the events are the result of a coordinated cyberattack on the U.S. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' "We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here. And we can be fairly confident in that because we know those things exist, and we’ve been looking for them in the past," Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, told Fox Business on Nov. 17. Secretary of State Marco Rubio concurred with Clayton's assessment. SWIFT ASSURANCES FROM OFFICIALS AFTER WAVE OF NATIONWIDE OUTAGES RAISES QUESTIONS, EXPERT SAYS "We are not under systemic attack…Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cybercriminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country…The American people should have confidence in that," Rubio said during a press conference in the Philippines the same day. In lieu of a coordinated cyberattack arranged by a foreign adversary such as Iran or North Korea, Walsh offered a counter hypothesis. FBI WARNS AI HACKERS CAN BREACH SYSTEMS IN UNDER 3 HOURS "The ability to attack is significantly lower cost than the cost of defending, [so] we create an asymmetry...in the advantage of the attacker," Walsh explained. "In the past, these types of attacks that were persistent would look for things, try to identify opportunities to take advantage of, and there was typically, you know, an iterative process, if you will, where there were humans in the loop and making changes. And now that essentially all happens instantaneously without the need for the AI attacker to reach back. So I think, yeah, I think that it's quite possible that some of the things we're beginning to see are certainly related to that, and we're going to see more of that," he told Fox News Digital. THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE Walsh also concurred with Rubio and Clayton's assessment regarding the lack of evidence pointing to a coordinated assault. Rather, he posited, much of the disruption is coming from critical industries recognizing vulnerabilities that could be exploited by AI-assisted hackers. Those disruptions, due to the increasingly centralized and interconnected digital world, may naturally cause ripple effects throughout linked systems. DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP "What we're seeing is more of a common architectural concern," Walsh explained. "It really is related in a way that we've spent decades connecting these legacy systems with modern applications. We've implemented cloud services, networks to improve efficiencies. And so we've created a lot of dependencies, and not just dependencies within the organization," Walsh told Fox News Digital. Those dependencies extend to large financial institutions, which Walsh also explained are highly interconnected. "It wouldn't be unusual that an event that might affect one financial institution might create transaction relations, related issues or other things, and other organizations that are in the process of clearing transactions and so on with these large, large infrastructures," he said. Walsh's recommended defense strategy is to build resiliency within the architecture of the nation's critical digital infrastructure. "The big issue that really we're beginning to, as a community, recognize that it's about resilience. It's about the architecture's ability to operate through events, and the systems have to isolate the events. They've got to protect what the essential services are," Walsh said. Besides working with silo networks and identifying users accessing those networks, there are also hardware fixes that chipmakers like Apple and Intel can implement. Walsh explained that chipmakers can install a cryptographic signature into their chips called a trusted platform module, or TPM. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "These are actual in the silicon cryptographic mechanisms so that you can latch on to those as the software and pass that what we'll call ‘root of trust’ up," he said.

articles.title: Newsom shredded for ‘hypocritical’ claim Trump 'sells' pardons after moving to spare 548 death row inmates
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom faces "arrogance and hypocrisy" backlash over calls to reform presidential pardon powers as he vows to spare 548 California death row inmates.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's calls for federal reforms to presidential pardon powers are garnering intense backlash for "hypocrisy" after he used his state-level executive powers to spare hundreds of death row inmates from receiving the death penalty. Trump vowed Monday to direct the Justice Department (DOJ) to seek the death penalty for child murderers and speed up federal executions after Newsom’s announcement. Online fury erupted after Newsom posted a video defending his decision to commute the death sentences of 548 criminals while accusing President Donald Trump of turning "the power of mercy into a business." "Gavin, is the arsonist calling for a ban on fire," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., posted on X. "Man who commuted 548 death row sentences is now deeply concerned about abuse of the pardon power." NEWSOM ORDERS CALIFORNIA’S MOST REVILED KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW – 10 OF THE WORST WHO COULD BENEFIT One X user noted how Trump "just told the DOJ to fast-track the death penalty for child killers and predators. [Gavin Newsom], on the other hand, is proudly defending his decision to spare 548 of the worst of the worst. "Tells you everything you need to know." Another user posted, "Are you f---ing kidding me? His arrogance and hypocrisy are immeasurable." "After pardoning everyone on death row in California, Newsom calls for reform of the president’s pardon powers," another wrote on X. "You can’t make this stuff up." Trump called out Newsom at the DOJ alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and family members of victims of the 548 death row inmates. He referred to the inmates as "the most evil monsters on the face of the Earth," and accused Newsom of stealing closure for the victims' families. Some of the crimes committed by inmates who will no longer face the death sentence include slaughtering entire families, torturing and murdering children and killing police officers. In Newsom’s video, he defended his decision to commute the death sentences to life without parole, accusing Trump of abusing his pardon powers. "Donald Trump doesn’t oppose mercy. He sells it," Newsom said in the video. "If you’re poor, Black or Brown, you get the needle. If you’re rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call." SLAIN FIREFIGHTER'S MOTHER PLEADS WITH TRUMP TO INTERVENE AFTER NEWSOM STOPS KILLER'S DEATH SENTENCE Trump issued 220 total pardons in his second term as president and 143 during his first term. While Trump has granted pardons to wealthy individuals and political allies, he has also pardoned Black Americans, most notably Alice Marie Johnson, who was serving a life sentence for drug trafficking and money laundering offenses before he commuted her sentence in 2018 and pardoned her in 2020. Trump has been criticized for his comments Tuesday that a pardon for Jensen Huang was "always an option" ahead of the Nvidia CEO's scheduled appearances before Congress next week following his re-instatement after claims he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. "I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vice President JD Vance told reporters Wednesday when asked about the potential. Part of the blowback against Newsom also stems from his decision to override California voters' rejection to abolish the death penalty, defending his clemency authority as an example of "when law as applied cannot be squared with justice." "And the Governor of CA should not be able to sell out crime victims and prosecutors by overriding juries, judges and the WILL of CA voters," a former Sacramento District Attorney posted to X. "Worst Governor in history." Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Monday he led 14 attorneys general in condemning Newsom’s plan, arguing Newsom had overridden juries, courts and California voters. Some critics have speculated Newsom's move to revoke California inmates death sentences is a tactic gearing up for his bid as the Democratic nominee for the 2028 presidential election. He is seen as one of the top candidates for the party. JAMES CARVILLE WARNS GAVIN NEWSOM FACES CALIFORNIA BAGGAGE IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN "You should think twice about this decision," a user said. "You may personally end up needing a Presidential pardon one day." A coalition of California prosecutors and victims’ relatives asked the state Supreme Court last week to halt Newsom’s plan, arguing that he failed to give families a chance to be heard before pursuing the commutations. Newsom asked the justices to act before his term ends in January. California voters rejected measures to abolish the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. The state last carried out an execution in 2006, and Newsom imposed a moratorium shortly after taking office in 2019. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. Fox News Digital's Jasmine Baehr and Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

articles.title: DOJ lawyers ordered to swarm 'frivolous' 97,000-lawsuit wave from ICE detainees
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche is mobilizing civil litigators across the Justice Department to fight 97,000 habeas corpus petitions from detained migrants.
articles.body: Attorney General Todd Blanche is mobilizing civil litigators across the Justice Department in an all-hands-on-deck push to fight tens of thousands of legal filings by detained migrants asking federal courts to review whether their imprisonment is lawful. Blanche issued a three-page memo Tuesday calling on attorneys working outside of immigration issues to assist in the lawsuits described by Blanche as "frivolous" and an attempt to "thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security." The pre-Thanksgiving memo comes as the Justice Department has been hit with 97, 000 habeas corpus petition filings since January 2025, including close to 10,000 new petitions filed since October. Typically, the Justice Department faces only a few hundred habeas corpus cases a year. As President Donald Trump has made mass deportations a centerpiece of his second administration, with Department of Homeland Security figures showing nearly 1.2 million illegal immigrants removed to date, the Justice Department has seen a wave of petitions. DHS TOUTS HIGHEST ICE DEPORTATIONS IN HISTORY, AS MULLIN SAYS AGENCY HAS BEEN ‘UNLEASHED’ The surge in lawsuits comes after the Trump administration changed its detention policy to deny bond hearings to migrants arrested inside the U.S. — even those who have lived in the country for years. Without access to bond hearings before immigration judges, detainees have turned directly to federal district courts to challenge their confinement. In a post on X sharing the memo, Blanche accused judges who have granted detained immigrants' habeas corpus petitions of being "corrupt" and seeking to "release criminal aliens back into communities and avoid deportation." "Many of the Department's U.S. Attorneys' Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts," Blanche wrote. "That is why it is imperative that all Department attorneys who litigate civil matters support prosecutors who have shouldered the burden of habeas petitions for nearly two years." SUPREME COURT TO SCRUTINIZE KEY PILLAR OF TRUMP DEPORTATION MACHINE IN BLOCKBUSTER CASE Blanche's memo calls on attorneys from four civil litigation divisions — Antitrust, Civil Rights, Civil, and Environment and Natural Resources — as well as the U.S. Trustees Program and senior leadership offices, including those of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general, to assist. Within the next 30 days, leadership from the respective divisions must submit an "aggressive appellate strategy" for tackling the habeas corpus claims and deploy attorneys to high-volume districts. The memo does not explicitly state how many of the department's roughly 2,000 civil litigators will be utilized. Blanche acknowledged that divisions are already carrying "a significant workload in light of personnel reduction." TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN COULD STRENGTHEN ADMIN'S HAND IN LOOMING SUPREME COURT FIGHT SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I also know that many attorneys have already volunteered or offered support in litigating habeas matters," Blanche wrote. "By ensuring that attorneys are assigned no more habeas matters than each attorney can adequately and zealously defend, combined with providing jurisdiction-specific resources, I hope to mitigate any significant disruption to attorneys' current dockets." Blanche's memo drew criticism from immigration attorneys, including Reza Mazaheri, who called the attorney general's characterization of judges as "corrupt" "slander." "If I walk into a courtroom and accuse a judge I disagree with of corruption, I would undoubtedly face disciplinary action," Mazaheri wrote on X. "In the public service sphere, the word 'corruption' has a distinct meaning." Meanwhile, Bridget Pranzatelli, a staff attorney at the National Immigration Project, told Newsweek that the influx of habeas corpus petitions is the result of a change in how the Trump administration interprets bond hearing statutes. "Many of them would have gotten a bond hearing before this administration suddenly changed its interpretation of a decades-old law to fill beds that private prison companies get paid for," Pranzatelli said in a statement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The memo comes as the U.S. Supreme Court prepares to hear arguments in early 2027 in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, a high-stakes challenge to the administration's mandatory detention policy. In October, the justices agreed to review a second U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that struck down ICE's policy of denying bond hearings to illegal immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for years. The court's decision — expected by late June or early July 2027 — will resolve a split among federal appeals courts and determine the fate of tens of thousands of pending habeas petitions.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: White House accuses South Korea of breaking promise to Trump as US tech giant faces $688M in fines
articles.summary: The White House says Seoul broke a promise to President Donald Trump on fair treatment for U.S. tech companies as regulators fined Coupang $688 million.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — The White House accused South Korea of breaking a promise to President Donald Trump to treat U.S. tech companies fairly, telling Fox News Digital that Seoul has since hit Coupang with hundreds of millions of dollars in fines. South Korean regulators have hit Coupang with roughly $688 million in fines, including a provisional $224 million penalty against its food delivery service, which was announced this month. A White House official said the administration opposes South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's alleged discrimination against U.S. companies and that the White House expects South Korea to keep its commitment to fair treatment for U.S. technology companies, including Coupang. EXPLOSIVE HOUSE REPORT REVEALS SECRET OPERATION INSIDE CHINA AT CENTER OF SOUTH KOREA'S FIGHT WITH US COMPANY A South Korean embassy official punched back at the White House's allegation that there was a direct targeting of Coupang, stating that the nation abides by the agreement with the Trump administration and is committed to a fair and nondiscriminatory business environment. "All investigations and decisions undertaken by the Korean government, including the recent fine imposed on food delivery service providers for anticompetitive conduct by the Korean Fair Trade Commission have been conducted lawfully and in accordance with applicable laws and regulations," a spokesperson for the Embassy of the Republic of Korea told Fox News Digital. "Furthermore, the right to seek legal remedies under the Korean law is fully guaranteed." The spokesperson explained that South Korea considers its strategic partnership with the U.S. its most important relationship, describing an alliance built on democracy, the rule of law and open markets, adding that Seoul will keep working closely with American policymakers to correct the record and deepen economic ties between the two countries. FORMER US AMBASSADOR SAYS SOUTH KOREA PROSECUTED HIM OVER SPEECH MADE ON AMERICAN SOIL Coupang, dubbed the "Amazon of South Korea" despite having no affiliation with Amazon, is the country's largest e-commerce company, known for its "Rocket Delivery" network that gets most orders to customers' doors the next day or even the same day. Although nearly all its business is in South Korea, Coupang is an American company. It is incorporated in Delaware, headquartered in Seattle and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The company was founded in 2010 by Korean American entrepreneur Bom Kim, who dropped out of Harvard Business School. FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS A State Department official told Fox News Digital the Korea Fair Trade Commission’s continued "assault" on American companies is threatening the broader potential of the U.S.-South Korea alliance. The State Department said it is actively evaluating a range of policy options to respond to what it calls discriminatory treatment. Yoon Suk Yeol, of the People Power Party, was elected president in 2022 but was impeached in December 2024, largely for his attempt to declare martial law. Lee Jae Myung, of the Democratic Party, lost to Yoon in the 2022 presidential election but was elected president in 2025. The Democratic Party holds a strong majority in South Korea’s National Assembly, giving the party control of both the presidency and the legislature for the first time since 2022. FORMER SOUTH KOREAN PRESIDENT YOON SUK YEOL SENTENCED TO 30 YEARS OVER NORTH KOREA DRONE FLIGHTS The Democratic Party is South Korea's main liberal party and favors progressive domestic policies. The country's conservatives have historically favored less engagement with North Korea and stronger ties with the U.S. Coupang said it has been the largest source of U.S. foreign direct investment in South Korea over the past decade, a claim House Republicans repeated in an April letter to South Korea's ambassador. The company said it drove more than $5 billion in overseas sales of American goods and services in 2025. WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA "As we have throughout the past year, Coupang continues to seek a constructive resolution that will strengthen the U.S.-Korea alliance, accelerating trade and investment that benefits both countries," Robert Porter, Coupang Inc.'s chief global affairs officer, told Fox News Digital in a statement. Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., who has been outspoken about South Korea's alleged discrimination against American companies, identified Biung-Ghi Ju, chair of the Korea Fair Trade Commission, as a key figure in the alleged practices. TRUMP ORDERS MAJOR CUT TO US-SOUTH KOREA DRILLS AS NORTH KOREA RAMPS UP MISSILE TESTS "For eight decades, America and Korea have benefited from an alliance purchased by sacrifice on the battlefield, joined by economic opportunity, and bolstered by mutual values," Issa told Fox News Digital. "The Lee government has the opportunity to repair or damage our relationship, and I hope he chooses the path of friendship, rather than continued confrontation." "But that is being put at risk by the anticompetitive policies of KFTC Chairman Ju that have unfairly targeted America’s tech industry and even individual American citizens," he added. SOUTH KOREAN PRESIDENT JUMPS TO INVEST IN MILITARY AFTER TRUMP CUTS JOINT EXERCISES In July, the House Judiciary Committee outlined a timeline of the South Korean government's scrutiny of Coupang, from a secret laptop recovery mission in China directed by South Korea's National Intelligence Service to the agency's request that the National Assembly pursue perjury charges against Harold Rogers, interim CEO of Coupang Corp., the company's South Korean subsidiary. A National Assembly committee filed the complaint, but Seoul police cleared Rogers in September and declined to refer the case to prosecutors. Rogers did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. "The Government of the Republic of Korea regrets that the interim staff report published by the U.S. House Judiciary Committee appears to be largely based on the unilateral assertions of Coupang and respectfully disagrees with several characterizations in the report," the embassy said.

articles.title: Presidential contender's 'remarkably tone-deaf’ move against Trump triggers parental uproar: 'Unconscionable'
articles.summary: Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker faces fierce school choice backlash after opting out of the federal scholarship tax credit. Critics cite politics.
articles.body: Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, widely believed to have presidential aspirations in 2028, is facing pushback from conservative education and school choice advocates over a move to opt out of a Trump federal scholarship tax credit program. Critics say the decision was made based on politics and not student outcomes. Pritzker announced Tuesday that the state will opt out of the Trump administration’s Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, refusing to allow Illinois students to receive scholarships funded through the federal school-choice initiative. In a press release, Pritzker argued that participating in what he labeled a "school voucher program" would siphon money and attention away from public education while subsidizing donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation or other characteristics. GOV KATHY HOCHUL SIGNS NEW YORK ONTO TRUMP'S SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DESPITE TEACHERS UNION OPPOSITION "At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education," Pritzker wrote. "We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics." Prominent conservative education activists and groups lambasted the move on social media, making the case that opting in takes nothing away from public schools and that Pritzker’s refusal simply blocks Illinois students from receiving privately funded scholarships while sending Illinois taxpayers’ charitable dollars to students in neighboring states. Many also pointed to abysmal test scores in Illinois and noted that Pritzker is siding with the state's powerful teachers unions. "It is a remarkably tone-deaf moment from Governor Pritzker, just before Thanksgiving, to deny 1.9 million K-12 students in Illinois access to life-changing educational resources as families are faced with rising costs and an affordability crisis," American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz said in a press release. "Make no mistake: The Education Freedom Tax Credit could have unlocked needed resources for families and students, but Governor Pritzker chose to let those resources go to other states." Schools for America Executive Director Jane McEnaney wrote on X, "Imagine being Governor of Illinois and hating Donald Trump more than you care about the educational opportunities of 1.9 million kids." PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS Pritzker's decision comes after three Democratic governors — New York’s Kathy Hochul, Colorado’s Jared Polis and New Mexico’s Michelle Lujan Grisham — agreed to enter the program, saying it brings millions of dollars in additional educational support to students without taking a single cent from public school or state budgets. The U. S. Department of Education responded to Pritzker’s press release as well, posting on X that by opting out of the program, Pritzker "just handed scholarship dollars from generous Illinois taxpayers to students in other states instead." Department of Education official Greg Dolan also weighed in on X, saying "the only true thing in this whole statement from @GovPritzker is his name." "May it live in infamy for so callously and cruelly turning his back on helping students in need," Dolan added. Erika Sanzi, senior director of communications at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital in an interview that Pritzker’s move was "unconscionable" and a "slap in the face" to parents, who will still be able to write off the taxes. But the money will not go to programs and resources for their children or other students in their state. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "You don't have to like the program, but can you at least describe it honestly and accurately?" Sanzi said about Pritzker’s statement. "They smear it as a voucher program because vouchers is the scary word but, like, putting aside the merits of vouchers, it's not a voucher program. "You can stay in the school you're in and still take advantage of these services. That's not a voucher program. I wish I could tell you I was surprised by Governor Pritzker. I am not, but I do think it's disappointing. And I certainly have seen outcry from families in the state that are just extremely frustrated not only by his decision, but by what he said in relation to his decision." Fox News Digital reached out to Pritzker’s office for comment. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The state's major teachers unions praised Pritzker’s move. Chicago Teachers Union and Illinois Federation of Teachers President Stacy Davis Gates applauded the governor for rejecting what she called "Trump's voucher scheme," arguing that "public dollars belong in public schools" and saying the program would pull money out of public education with "zero oversight." Illinois Education Association President Karl Goeke similarly thanked Pritzker for rejecting vouchers, calling them a "scam" that sends public money to private schools lacking the same testing standards as public schools.

articles.title: Trump could avoid Dems' ‘extreme’ amnesty push by signing immigration reform before new Congress
articles.summary: House Republicans say President Donald Trump could sign the Dignity Act this Congress, but warn delay would bring a bill more like an amnesty bill.
articles.body: House Republicans are optimistic that President Donald Trump could sign a bipartisan immigration reform bill before Democrats take control of Congress. They warn that if the president waits until January it could result in legislation containing more "extreme" language that opens the door for amnesty. "Yes, it's going to happen under this Congress," Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., told Fox News Digital, pointing to the country's labor shortages and Republicans' declining support among Hispanic voters as reasons to pursue immigration reform. "I think it's a win-win for a country, we get a much-needed workforce while providing some accountability for misbehavior." Bacon's remarks come after Trump signaled during a recent "60 Minutes" interview that he would be open to immigration reform, potentially creating an opportunity for lawmakers to advance the Dignity Act, a bill introduced by Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., in 2025. WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS The legislation, which now has over a dozen Republican co-sponsors, would provide certain undocumented immigrants who meet eligibility requirements with renewable legal status and work authorization, without establishing a direct pathway to citizenship. However, Bacon warned that delaying the legislation until the 120th Congress, when Democrats will control both chambers, could result in a more expansive immigration package. "Unfortunately, I think the Dems will make it more like an amnesty bill," Bacon told Fox News Digital. "They'll probably go to another extreme." Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., added to Fox News Digital that "there is no better solution on the table that will get support from both parties while simultaneously standing in the way of the Democrats' looming amnesty-ridden citizenship-for-all alternative." "The best way to see the work the administration is doing continue into the next two years while Democrats are in control of both houses is to pass a Republican-led immigration plan before January," Stutzman continued. GOP INFIGHTING ERUPTS OVER IMMIGRATION BILL THAT WOULD SHIELD MILLIONS FROM DEPORTATION Salazar previously told Fox News Digital that Trump's willingness to discuss immigration reform could create an opportunity to advance her legislation before Republicans lose control of Congress. "I think that this is a very good window to concentrate on something that even the president said that he was willing to work with the Dems, which is immigration," Salazar said. TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS The bill's original sponsor also expressed hope that Trump could make immigration reform a defining part of his presidential legacy, comparing the opportunity to Abraham Lincoln's role in ending slavery. Senate Democrats., like Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital that he would be willing to work with Salazar on pushing for the immigration bill. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I'm here to try to bring as many protections as I can to these families." Gallego told Fox News Digital. "Let's get it going, we're willing to work with anybody to try to keep these families together." The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Ada Colau llama a las mujeres a votar para frenar a Vox: "Continúa negando la violencia machista y lleva a algunos agresores en sus listas"
articles.standfirst: La candidata de Frente Amplio a la Presidencia del Gobierno ha lanzado este mensaje durante su entrevista con Carlos Franganillo en 'Informativos Telecinco', coincidiendo con el Día Internacional de la Eliminación de la Violencia contra la Mujer
articles.summary: La candidata de Frente Amplio a la Presidencia del Gobierno ha lanzado este mensaje durante su entrevista con Carlos Franganillo en 'Informativos Telecinco', coincidiendo con el Día Internacional de la Eliminación de la Violencia contra la Mujer
articles.body: La candidata de Frente Amplio a la Presidencia del Gobierno en las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre, Ada Colau, ha abordado algunos de los principales asuntos de la campaña electoral en una entrevista con Carlos Franganillo en 'Informativos Telecinco'. La exalcaldesa de Barcelona ha hablado sobre la fragmentación de la izquierda, la ausencia de Podemos en la nueva coalición, la lucha contra la violencia machista y las propuestas de su formación en materia de vivienda y derechos sociales. Uno de los asuntos centrales de la conversación ha sido precisamente la configuración del Frente Amplio, una formación que nació tras la convocatoria electoral de Pedro Sánchez y que aspira a reunir a distintas organizaciones de la izquierda. Ada Colau ha defendido la necesidad de construir una alternativa política que tenga representación en el Congreso más allá del Partido Socialista. La candidata ha explicado que, tras participar en la manifestación del 25 de noviembre por la eliminación de la violencia contra las mujeres, escuchó a muchas personas reclamar "una fuerza fuerte que entrara en el Congreso de izquierda transformadora, más allá del Partido Socialista". En este sentido, ha reivindicado el trabajo realizado para poner en marcha el proyecto y ha destacado que el Frente Amplio reúne a quince formaciones políticas, algo que considera "un éxito". Preguntada por la ausencia de Podemos en esta nueva alianza de izquierdas, Ada Colau ha reconocido que la formación que lidera Irene Montero tuvo la oportunidad de incorporarse, pero finalmente decidió no hacerlo. "Podemos no quiso estar, se le invitó hasta el último momento", ha asegurado. La candidata de Frente Amplio también ha explicado que su disposición a liderar el proyecto no era una condición innegociable. "Yo en todo momento ofrecí, incluso si había otra persona de mayor consenso", ha señalado, antes de añadir que estaba dispuesta a dar un paso atrás si su presencia suponía un obstáculo para alcanzar un acuerdo. "Estaba dispuesta a apartarme para que no fuera ese el obstáculo, pero cuando alguien no quiere, pues no se le puede obligar", ha sentenciado. Sobre el escenario político que se abre tras las elecciones, Ada Colau ha defendido que es importante identificar las prioridades de la campaña. "El adversario es que no haya un Gobierno de Partido Popular y Vox", ha afirmado. La lucha contra la violencia machista también ha ocupado una parte importante de la entrevista, que ha coincidido con el Día Internacional de la Eliminación de la Violencia contra las Mujeres. Ada Colau ha aprovechado la ocasión para hacer un llamamiento a la participación electoral femenina el próximo 29 de noviembre. "Todas las mujeres acudan a votar en masa", ha reclamado la candidata, que ha advertido de que existe un partido con opciones de entrar en el Gobierno que "sigue negando a día de hoy la violencia machista". La exalcaldesa de Barcelona ha recordado que acababa de participar en la manifestación celebrada este 25 de noviembre. "Había miles de mujeres y creo que en este contexto, de casi 50 mujeres asesinadas en lo que va de año, no nos vamos a callar ni nos vamos a rendir hasta que sean 0", ha manifestado. Ada Colau ha acusado a Vox de poner en riesgo los avances en igualdad y de respaldar a personas condenadas por violencia machista. "No solo niegan la violencia machista, sino que avalan a los agresores y los encubren. De hecho, llevan a algunos agresores condenados por violencia machista en sus listas y esto creo que las mujeres de este país no lo podemos permitir", ha declarado. La vivienda ha sido otro de los grandes bloques de la entrevista. Ada Ada Colau ha reconocido que este ámbito ha sido uno de los puntos débiles de la gestión del Gobierno y ha defendido la necesidad de introducir cambios para facilitar el acceso a una vivienda. Entre las medidas que plantea el Frente Amplio ha mencionado la intervención de los precios del alquiler y la posibilidad de prorrogar los contratos o establecer su carácter indefinido. La candidata también ha querido lanzar un mensaje de tranquilidad a los pequeños propietarios, diferenciándolos de los grandes fondos de inversión. "Pueden estar perfectamente tranquilos", ha asegurado. Ada Colau ha explicado que su formación considera pequeños propietarios a quienes tienen tres o cuatro viviendas, una situación que, según ha señalado, puede responder a circunstancias familiares habituales: disponer de una residencia principal, una casa en el pueblo o una vivienda para los hijos. En este sentido, ha insistido en que el Frente Amplio no pretende aumentar la presión fiscal sobre este colectivo. "A esos pequeños propietarios no solo no les vamos a subir impuestos, sino que nuestra intención es bajar los impuestos para la adquisición de la propiedad de una primera vivienda", ha afirmado. La propuesta de la formación se dirige, en cambio, contra los grandes fondos que acumulan un elevado número de inmuebles. Ada Colau ha defendido que su partido quiere poner "todo el énfasis en los especuladores" y ha señalado a trece fondos que, según sus cifras, concentran unas 100.000 viviendas. Su intención, ha explicado, es expropiar esos inmuebles para destinarlos al alquiler asequible y facilitar así el acceso a la vivienda a un mayor número de personas. Por último, Carlos Franganillo ha preguntado a la candidata por las recientes medidas sociales aprobadas o anunciadas por el Gobierno, entre ellas la ampliación del permiso por fallecimiento de un familiar directo hasta los diez días y la ayuda de 200 euros por cada menor. Ada Colau ha valorado positivamente estas iniciativas y ha atribuido a Yolanda Díaz el impulso de la medida relacionada con el duelo. "Son medidas buenas las que se han aprobado, como las del duelo por la muerte de un familiar directo hasta diez días. Es una medida impulsada por Yolanda Díaz y que estaba preparada de hacía tiempo y efectivamente se podría haber aprobado antes", ha señalado. También ha cuestionado que el PSOE haya mantenido bloqueada durante años la propuesta del ministro Bustinduy para conceder una ayuda de 200 euros por cada menor y que ahora la anuncie en un mitin electoral. "Nosotros defendemos esas medidas, las hemos peleado", ha recordado. Preguntada por si considera que los socialistas están intentando apropiarse de las propuestas de su formación para atraer a sus votantes, Ada Colau ha respondido sin mostrar reparos a que incorporen esas iniciativas a su programa. "A mí me parece bien que nos copien las medidas, pero que no se quede en una promesa electoral", ha concluido.
